entry.title: How 10x engineers play the system
entry.summary: And some actually useful tips
entry.content:
I just saw this Tweet:

~9.5% of software engineers do virtually nothing: Ghost Engineers (0.1x-ers) — Yegor Denisov-Blanch

Although I haven’t seen the details of the analysis method, I’m rather certain that this analysis to a large degree just looked at lines of code as a performance metric. I’m against any performance metric in software engineering as it’s just so easy to game the system. Let me show you how to become a 10x engineer 😄

Please note: Some of those add value, but the amount of value added likely does not correlate with the metric.

Lines of Code

  • Make automated formatting changes. Change your mind about which type of formatting you like best for extra lines.
  • Commit auto-generated files like an OpenAPI JSON schema file.
  • Make super long comments.

Number of Commits

  • Just work on tiny changes
  • Don’t finish your work — just add the fix later
  • Add tests in a separate commit

Number of PRs

Basically the same as for commits. If it’s not about merged PRs, then you can just open PRs and close them again 😄

On a more serious note, there are also some hints that can boost your productivity:

Use Asynchronous Communication Wisely

E-Mails should be seen asynchronously and I tend to see the beginning of a chat conversation the same way. If you’re not involved in a chat discussion, it can be valuable to not answer an incoming message right away. I haven’t used this on purpose so far, but I’ve noticed when I didn’t answer a chat message within ~10 minutes, quite often the problem was either resolved or there was valuable additional information.

However, it’s also helpful if you can give tips quickly. So you need to decide if it’s better to continue your current work or to interrupt and support a team member.

Use LLMs for Code Monkey work

LLMs such as ChatGPT can do some tedious tasks very well. For example, I tend to forget how to do a negative lookahead with regular expressions (RegEx). Instead of looking it up, I now just ask ChatGPT.

Another example is formatting diffs. Sometimes test cases fail and the diff output is hard to read. There are nice libraries such as pytest-icdiff, but that doesn’t always help.

The third category is debugging. Sometimes I’m stuck with super dumb mistakes as I went blind to a typo. Giving ChatGPT the Traceback and the relevant part of the code typically helps to find the issue.

Learn your Tools

It sounds stupid, but there might be some tiny improvements that would help you very often through the day. Things that pop to my mind:

  • How to jump to a file within your editor without using the mouse
  • How to jump to a line within a file
  • Git blame within your editor. Also how to go to the code change before the current change
  • Auto-save the current file

By the way, I’m not a big fan of pair programming. But it’s nice to learn such small tricks.

entry.title: Awesome PR processes in 7 easy steps
entry.summary: In this article I’ll describe some patterns I’ve noticed that help to make the pull request (PR) process smooth and productive.
entry.content:
In this article I’ll describe some patterns I’ve noticed that help to make the pull request (PR) process smooth and productive.

№ 1: Keep changes minimal

It’s easier to review one file than ten. It’s easier to review 30 lines of code than 300.

But it’s not only that. If you make many unrelated changes, it’s hard for reviewers to wrap their head around those changes. Why did you do them? Why are they necessary?

Even worse: Every single change might be something to discuss.

For this reason, it’s helpful to only do stylistic changes in lines that you have to touch anyway. If you notice an issue on your way, rather open another PR to fix that issue.

One way to reduce PR sizes quite a lot is to make a separate PR with tests that should already succeed. Maybe the behavior was changed just slightly and one of your tests would look almost the same for an old version. Then you can make a first PR to add the test that should work and provide value on its own. In the second PR you make the adjustments to that test.

Another way to reduce PR sizes is to make refactoring PRs. When you add a complex new feature you might need to restructure the code. This restructuring does not change the behavior of the code, but makes it more flexible so that your actual changes can get added.

№ 2: Document Intention

A PR has a title and a summary. Use both to describe your intention. Not what you did or how you did it — both are documented in the code. But what did you try to achieve?

This is not only important for the reviewer, but also for you in the future. You might stumble over a line of code and go back in the commit history. When you wonder why you made this PR, you should give yourself enough context.

Let’s have a look at some random ones:

№ 3: Ask for specific Feedback

What should the reviewer do? Some examples might be:

  • Checking if Acceptance Criteria (ACs) are fulfilled: You can list those explicitly
  • Correctness of a specific part: Maybe you have doubts if you did an aspect of the PR correctly. Point that out!
  • Maintainability and Code Style
  • Knowledge Sharing: Maybe you don’t really need feedback, but rather want your reviewer to get familiar with a certain part of the code or a specific way to write code / tests.

This is done pretty well on Code Review Stack Exchange.

№ 4: Add Tests or Proof of Testing

A test can show very clearly how a feature is intended to be used. Additionally, it ensures that it keeps working in future.

In some cases you cannot write tests or the effort would be unreasonable. For example, when I write code for Django Admin I typically try to attach a screenshot that shows the change. This is typically easier and better than writing a unit test.

In both cases: When I’m reviewing code and I have doubts if something works, a test or proof of testing does wonders. It then means that I have to be rather certain that something does not work. So it tips the scales for approval of the PR.

№ 5: Use prefixes in titles

I first came across this in the scipy development workflow:

API: an (incompatible) API change
BENCH: changes to the benchmark suite
BLD: change related to building SciPy
BUG: bug fix
DEP: deprecate something, or remove a deprecated object
DEV: development tool or utility
DOC: documentation
ENH: enhancement
MAINT: maintenance commit (refactoring, typos, etc.)
REV: revert an earlier commit
STY: style fix (whitespace, PEP8)
TST: addition or modification of tests
REL: related to releasing SciPy

Examples for PR titles in that project are:

ENH: differentiate: add array API support to jacobian and hessian
TST: optimize.linprog/milp: add tests for various bug reports
API: stats.{PermutationMethod,BootstrapMethod}: transition to rng (SPEC 7)
MAINT: linalg.interpolative: normalize rng argument with default_rng
MAINT: bump array-api-extra
BUG: guard distance_wrap directives

The prefix sets the expectation for the PR. In companies, you might have a tracking system and use the ticket number as the prefix.

№ 6: Establish a Commenting Culture in the Team

If a PR is long it happens regularly to me that 95% of the PR is obviously good and should be merged. There is just a small part where I’m uncertain about which means I will not approve the PR.

It’s good to add comments on that part in such situations. It shows the PR author that you have a look and might give them ideas how to improve the PR to make it easier to review.

The comments should be full sentences and be constructive. If you can make an explicit suggestion to fix an issue, do it!

3 rules of a good pull request comment Nowadays it seems all the development happens on Github. There is so called Github flow where you submit pull requests…

№ 7: PRs have top priority

An open and ready PR should almost always have priority. Before you start any new work, ensure that others can finish their stuff. It might be that you have doubts about the change — that’s why we have rule №6. Ask the PR author about that. Dangling PRs are frustrating and demotivating. Don’t do that to your team.

entry.title: Pagination done right
entry.summary: offset, limit, order, filtering, performance, and UX
entry.content:
In times of infinite scrolling, you might be tempted to think that pagination doesn’t matter. But even infinite scrolling sites use pagination under the hood for their backends. They automatically load the next “page” and append it to the bottom.

The Basics: Offset, limit, and Order!

When you implement pagination, you need three elements:

  • Offset: Which element is the first you want to see in the response? For the first call, the offset should be 0.
  • Limit: This limits the maximum amount of elements shown. Even when the user requests something huge, you should have a maximum in the backend that you enforce.
  • Order: It’s crucial to choose a consistent ordering. I like to order by creation time, with the oldest object first. This way the user will see the most recent ones at the end and not have skipped anything. However, it depends on your application what is most reasonable.

The common terminology is that given an ordered result set, the first offset elements are skipped. Then up to limit elements are shown.

Filtering

While filtering is typically done in the same context, it’s very different. And it can be way more complicated. Filtering deserves its own article 😄

Performance

We need pagination for performance:

  • Network transfer times: The full dataset could be huge. It might take several seconds to transfer everything in one big result set. Even worse, the time is not predictable, so we would have to optimize those endpoints again and again. Instead, we can just paginate and know that the network time is always roughly the same.
  • DB speed: Having a small (offset+limit) helps the DB to be fast. Most of the time the users are only interested in the first few results anyway. Just keep in mind that if the user actually goes to the end, the last pages essentially mean to the DB that it needs to compute the whole result set.

UX

  • Total element count: Showing a total element count is nice for users, and it might also be a good idea to return it in your API.
  • Show previous and next as buttons: When I scroll through large datasets, I like it when the buttons exist and when they are always at the same location.

entry.title: The Python PDF Ecosystem in 2024
entry.summary: Which libraries should you use for which use case?
entry.content:
The Python PDF ecosystem is a mess. There are tons of packages on PyPI, but many of them are inactive. As I had the dubious fortune of having to work with PDF documents a couple of times in my career as a Python developer, let me guide you through this jungle.

Although people have all kinds of Python/PDF-related issues, most are around three topics: (1) Read text from PDF documents (2) Read tables from PDF documents (3) Generate PDF documents. I’ll focus on those.

Full disclosure: I am the maintainer of pypdf and PyPDF2. I’m also part of the py-pdf organization which aims to improve the Python ecosystem around PDF files. It contains pypdf, fpdf2, pdfly, and pypdf_table_extraction. I am biased when it comes to those libraries.

The Top Libraries by PyPI Download Statistics 🏆

The PyPI download statistics from March 2024 (30 days, ending in 2024–03–01 09:13:24). In brackets are the variants that were added to the download count.

Reference projects:

  • 1. boto3, downloaded 1,136,326,177×: A library to interact with AWS
  • 2. botocore, downloaded 522,672,231×: Used by boto3
  • 3. urllib3, downloaded 464,629,985×: A library for making HTTP requests
  • 4. requests, downloaded 385,781,127×: A library for making HTTP requests
  • 5. certifi, downloaded 354,125,620×: Mozilla’s root certificates
  • 6. wheel, downloaded 351,980,457×: Building Python packages
  • 7. pip, downloaded 351,883,200×
  • 8. typing-extensions, downloaded 344,505,419×
  • 9. charset-normalizer, downloaded 328,506,796×
  • 10. setuptools, downloaded 327,273,028×
  • 61. pytest, downloaded 92,853,947×
  • 227. black, downloaded 26,976,103×
  • 270. flake8, downloaded 22,282,064×
  • 518. ruff, downloaded 8,455,716×

The PDF projects:

  • 483. pypdf (1498 questions on SO), downloaded 9,386,480× (pypdf2, pypdf3, pypdf4)
  • 795. reportlab (1303 questions on SO), downloaded 4,692,632×
  • 981. pdfminer-six (490 questions on SO), downloaded 3,294,764× (pdfminer, pdfminer2)
  • 1198. pymupdf (314 questions on SO), downloaded 2,167,085×
  • 1240. fpdf2 (94 questions on SO), downloaded 2,005,313× (fpdf)
  • 1243. pikepdf (31 questions on SO), downloaded 1,995,403×
  • 1514. weasyprint (264 questions on SO), downloaded 1,346,313×
  • 1597. pdf2image (71 questions on SO), downloaded 1,202,507×
  • 1725. pdfkit (1099 questions on SO), downloaded 1,038,023×
  • 1742. xhtml2pdf (236 questions on SO), downloaded 1,015,678×
  • 1859. pdfplumber, downloaded 896,970×
  • 1909. pypdfium2, downloaded 849,968×
  • 2131. pyhanko (7 questions on SO), downloaded 691,196×
  • 2329. rpaframework-pdf, downloaded 562,711×
  • 3002. Apache tika (1295 questions on SO), downloaded 334,184×
  • 3035. camelot-py (205 questions on SO), downloaded 329,521×
  • 3350. tabula-py (143 questions on SO), downloaded 269,182×
  • 3411. img2pdf, downloaded 260,442×
  • 3869. pdftopng, downloaded 201,993×
  • 4057. pdfrw, downloaded 183,801× — inactive, use pypdf
  • 5208. sphinxcontrib-svg2pdfconverter, downloaded 124,449×
  • 5420. pdf2docx, downloaded 115,100×
  • 6620. rst2pdf, downloaded 71,128×
  • 6961. ocrmypdf, downloaded 64,633×
  • 6962. wkhtmltopdf, downloaded 64,615×
  • 7034. pdftotext, downloaded 62,963×
  • 7103. docx2pdf, downloaded 61,637×

PyPI download statistics don’t represent popularity properly. People who have automatic Continuous Integration (CI) systems / build systems download their packages again and again. They easily make it appear as if the package is used all the time. That is an inherent skew towards libraries/frameworks used in web development.

Some projects have Anaconda packages and even Debian / Ubuntu packages. That reduces the number of PyPI downloads.

There are some libraries where the users should migrate:

  • Use pypdf: There is no good reason to use PyPDF2, PyPDF3, PyPDF4 anymore
  • Use pdfminer-six: Why do people still use pdfminer?
  • Use fpdf2: fpdf was last updated in 2018 and doesn’t support Python 3.9.

Comparison to 2023

Since last year boto3 got +126%, pytest +74%, and black +69%. I assume the boto3 numbers are massively inflated by CI systems, but the Python ecosystem could have gotten +70% more usage due to the AI hype.

Given this context, pypdf and its variants have +82%. The pypdf download numbers have exploded while PyPDF2 only increased a tiny bit. PyPDF3 and PyPDF4 are irrelevant.

Hot and new are pikepdf (+321%!), pdfplumber (+131%) and pypdfium2 wasn’t even in the stats.

pikepdf is an allrounder tool based on QPDF, but it has two severe limitations: pikepdf cannot extract text and pikepdf is not a PDF generation library. It can linearize/compress/normalize PDFs.

pdfplumber is based on pdfminer.six and can extract detailed information about the font/position of each character on every page. pdfplumber can extract tables, but your mileage will vary.

reportlab got +114%, while fpdf2 (including fpdf) only got +62%. I wonder why that is.

Text Extraction from PDF Documents 📖

If you simply want to get the complete text of a PDF page, but don’t care about its exact position, my PDF text extraction benchmark shows the best choices:

  • pypdfium2 (Apache-2.0 or BSD-3-Clause license): It’s fast and the text extraction is very good. The only downside might be that it might be hard to install as it relies on PDFium (Apache 2.0 license) which is a C++ project.
  • Apache Tika (Apache-2.0 license) is a little bit slower and a little bit worse in text extraction quality, but still excellent. It is a Java project and the server has to be started, so the first run might be slow.
  • PyMuPDF (GNU AFFERO GPL 3.0 / Commercial), also called “fitz”, is on-par with Tika. It relies on MuPDF by Artifex Software, Inc. under AGPLv3. It’s a C project and thus might come with the same installation issues as pypdfium2 / tika. The commercial license is something you need to check.
  • pypdf (BSD license) is a pure Python project. I became the maintainer of it in April 2022 and since then we have improved its quality a lot. Its text extraction speed is roughly 10x — 20x slower than the one of pypdfium2/tika/PyMuPDF. The text extraction quality is roughly the same, but the other three projects deal better with whitespaces. PyPDF2, PyPDF3, PyPDF4 should no longer be used. They are forks of pypdf which are far behind in development and no longer maintained. Use pypdf. We have also added a layout mode for text extraction.

If you want some extra information, e.g. which font was used for a specific word or where exactly the character is on the page, then use pdfminer.six or pdfplumber (built on pdfminer.six). Their text extraction quality is worse than the one of the other four libraries, though.

Extracting tables is another special case of text extracting. camelot-py, tabula-py, and pdfplumber approach this.

A completely different topic is extracting text from images (or scanned PDF documents). That is OCR. Try tesseract for that task. Since ChatGPT arrived it might be worth using it to extract tables in a reasonable format.

Generating PDF Documents 🔨

I see two reasonable choices to create PDF documents:

  1. Create the raw PDF from code: reportlab is well known, but fpdf2 works in a very similar way. The project recently joined the py-pdf organization and is actively maintained free and open-source software (FOSS).
  2. Create an intermediate format and convert it to PDF: There are several options, e.g. pdfkit or xhtml2pdf (using HTML) or pdflatex (using LaTeX). There are certainly way more, e.g. docx2pdf. I haven’t used those, though.
  3. Images: You can convert SVG to PDF via sphinxcontrib-svg2pdfconverter and other images via img2pdf.

In all cases, you can add metadata with pypdf.

Reading and Writing PDF Metadata 📝

Reading and writing PDF metadata with Python can be done with multiple libraries:

  • pypdf, see the docs on how to read/write PDF metadata
  • PyMuPDF (docs)
  • pikepdf (docs)

Signing a PDF Document

pyhanko is the only option here.

Python PDF Applications 👩💻

  • pdfly: View metadata, create a 2-up booklet, compress a PDF, extract text, and concatenate PDFs.
  • pdfalyzer: In-depth analysis of PDF files

Are you curious about last year's overview?

The Python PDF Ecosystem in 2023 Which libraries should you use for which use case?

entry.title: Designing Event-Driven Systems in Local Python Applications
entry.summary: An event-driven software architecture can help you write cleaner code. Most software engineers are likely familiar with pre-defined event systems such as those provided by frontend frameworks/languages: keypress in JavaScript, bind in Tkinter, or keyPressEvent in PyQt/PySide. You might also know Django Signals, or have heard of Apache …
entry.content:
An event-driven software architecture can help you write cleaner code. Most software engineers are likely familiar with pre-defined event systems such as those provided by frontend frameworks/languages: keypress in JavaScript, bind in Tkinter, or keyPressEvent in PyQt/PySide. You might also know Django Signals, or have heard of Apache Kafka or Google Cloud Pub/Sub in the context of distributed systems.

An event-driven software architecture does not have to be that complicated.

The components of an event-driven system are straightforward: You have events, producers of those events, and consumers of the events. Then you need some glue code that forwards the events from the producers to the consumers. This is called the event registry.

Building Event-Driven Software

I recently started building the flitz file manager to dip my toes into the development of graphical user interfaces with Python. I started with the Tkinter framework but recognized it was not a good match. Porting to Qt is hard as I have a tight coupling with Tkinter.

For example, when changing the current path via the URL bar, I want the listed documents to be changed. Flitz also has an “up” button. When it is clicked, the current path shown in the URL bar is changed and the shown documents in the details pane are changed.

Conceptually, the code could look like this:

class FileExplorer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.current_path = Path(".")

        # Show the UI widgets
        details_view = DetailsView(self)
        url_bar = UrlBar(self)
        up_button = UpButton(self)


class UrlBar:
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.root = root
        self.text = str(self.root.current_path)

    def on_keypress_enter(self):
        # Let the main application know that the path changed
        self.root.current_path = Path(self.text)

        # Trigger follow-up changes
        self.root.details_view.refresh()
        self.refresh()

    def refresh(self):
        self.text = str(self.root.current_path)


class UpButton:
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.root = root

    def on_press(self):
        # Let the main application know that the path changed
        self.root.current_path = self.root.current_path.parent

        # Trigger follow-up changes
        self.root.details_view.refresh()
        self.root.url_bar.refresh()


class DetailsView:
    def refresh(self):
        """Show the files from the root.current_path."""

You can see that there is logic duplication in UpButton.on_press and UrlBar.on_keypress_enter. Such duplicated code becomes harder to maintain as the application grows. At some point, someone will forget to update/refresh one GUI widget of the application.

Instead, you can define a set_current_path function:

class FileExplorer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.current_path = Path(".")

        # Show the UI widgets
        self.details_view = DetailsView(self)
        self.url_bar = UrlBar(self)
        self.up_button = UpButton(self)

    def set_current_path(self, current_path):
        self.current_path = current_path
        self.details_view.refresh()
        self.url_bar.refresh()


class UrlBar:
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.root = root
        self.text = str(self.root.current_path)

    def on_keypress_enter(self):
        self.root.set_current_path(Path(self.text))


class UpButton:
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.root = root

    def on_press(self):
        self.root.set_current_path(self.root.current_path.parent)


class DetailsView:
    def refresh(self):
        """Show the files from the root.current_path."""

The next part we want to improve is the locality of the code. Meaning that one component should have all of its code in one place. Having several unrelated lines in set_current_path makes it harder to change those components and inspect if they do the right thing. I mean, how do you know if there is a component that should be touched in set_current_path without checking the code of every single component?

from pathlib import Path


# events.py
class Event:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.listeners = []

    def consumed_by(self, listener):
        self.listeners.append(listener)

    def produce(self):
        for listener in self.listeners:
            listener()


current_path_changed = Event("current_path_changed")


# Remaining code:
class FileExplorer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.current_path = Path(".")
        self.event_registry = {}  # Event registry to hold component listeners

        # Show the UI widgets
        self.details_view = DetailsView(self)
        self.url_bar = UrlBar(self)
        self.up_button = UpButton(self)

    def set_current_path(self, current_path):
        self.current_path = current_path
        current_path_changed.produce()


class UrlBar:
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.root = root
        self.text = str(self.root.current_path)
        current_path_changed.consumed_by(self.refresh)

    def on_keypress_enter(self):
        self.root.set_current_path(Path(self.text))

    def refresh(self):
        self = self.root.url_bar
        self.text = str(self.root.current_path)
        print(f"UrlBar refreshed")


class UpButton:
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.root = root

    def on_press(self):
        self.root.set_current_path(self.root.current_path.parent.resolve())


class DetailsView:
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.root = root
        current_path_changed.consumed_by(self.refresh)

    def refresh(self):
        """Show the files from the root.current_path."""
        print(
            f"Refreshing details view with files from {self.root.current_path}"
        )


# Example usage:
explorer = FileExplorer()
explorer.up_button.on_press()

You can also use a library like blinker for that.

And that’s it. You’ve seen an event-driven system 🎉

In this case, the registry is every single Event object.

That’s simple — why does Apache Kafka exist?

Kafka is used in large distributed systems. That especially means that you have a network with latency and errors. Consumers might come and go; just like producers.

Gotcha, but why do we need blinker?

  • Multi-threading

  • Disconnecting Consumers

  • Attached data: In this simple example the event didn’t come with any data. That is different in many use cases.

Terminology — many words for the same concepts

Events and signals are the same thing. Similarly, we have a couple of pairs that belong together:

Event Action Follow-up Comment
Event Publisher Subscriber Apache Kafka, Google Pub/Sub
Event Producer Consumer RabbitMQ, Spring Cloud Stream
Event Dispatch Listener JavaScript
Signal Sender Receiver Blinker

Pitfalls of Event-Driven Systems

  • Order: You should design your event-driven system in a way that the order of execution of the consumers does not matter.

  • Infinite Loops: Event A might cause Event B which causes Event A.

TL;DR

  • What: Event-driven systems have events, parts of code that produce those events, and other parts that consume those events.

  • Why: It’s useful to decouple the senders from the receivers. That increases maintainability.

  • How: The simplest way to implement event-driven software is by using global objects for the signals. Those are then used by the producers and automatically call the consumers. Libraries like blinker can help. If you are in a distributed system things become more complicated.

entry.title: What’s hot and what’s not in Python, August 2023
entry.summary: An analysis of PyPI download statistics
entry.content:
The Python Package Index (PyPI) tracks the downloaded packages. I’ve checked the monthly statistics for the two time frames:

  • 1st of June to 30th of June and
  • 1st of July to 31st of July

and compared them.

It’s important to realize that download statistics do not tell you anything about the code quality and only give a small indication of popularity. The download statistics get pushed if people regularly download packages through their Continuous Integration (CI) systems for testing their own software. Being a dependency of a popular package certainly helps. And just being an indirect dependency by many packages is typically also not exciting. There is a reason why requests and boto3 are typically in the TOP-10.

Top Newcomers

In the following, I tried to group packages if multiple newcomers are just the cause of another change.

  1. № 134, downloaded 30232921x: jsonschema-specifications. That pulled rpds-py and referencing up as well. And the reason it came up that quickly is because the jsonschema package was popular before. Those became a dependency in February, but only in July were the releases. Yes, multiple releases.
  2. № 307, downloaded 12068823x: annotated-types — PEP-593 added typing.Annotated. Python is improved by “Python Enhancement Proposals” — short: PEPs. This package makes a PEP that was introduced in Python 3.9 usable for normal users. That is exciting 😍
  3. № 1253, downloaded 1392567x: google-re2, a drop-in replacement for the re module. It’s been on version 1.0 in 2020 already. I don’t know why it suddenly got such a boost in downloads. Likely because something from the Google Cloud packages now depends on it.
  4. № 1539, downloaded 912974x: wexpect, a Windows variant of pexpect. A module for spawning child applications. This one is even more confusing. It’s hardly a newcomer. I’m also not aware of any big packages now depending on it.
  5. № 1921, downloaded 582748x: LangSmith, a Python client for interacting with the LangSmith platform. LangChain is a tool for LLMs. You know, the ChatGPT hype.
  6. № 2147, downloaded 467417x: itables, Turn your Python DataFrames into Interactive Tables
  7. № 2212, downloaded 443474x: uproot3, is a reader and a writer of the ROOT file format.
  8. № 2220, downloaded 440534x: awkward0 a pure Python+Numpy library for manipulating complex data structures as you would Numpy arrays
  9. № 2240, downloaded 432486x: coffea is a package for the typical needs of a high-energy collider physics (HEP) experiment analysis
  10. № 2247, downloaded 429644x: boost-histogram — Python bindings for Boost::Histogram.

Top Trending

  1. +4082, current rank is 282: pydantic-core — the data validation library pydantic released a 2.0 version which had heavy refactoring and tons of news / podcasts around it. pydantic is used by FastAPI and many other projects. If you don’t know it, it’s somewhat similar to attrs.
  2. +2508, current rank is 2089: awkward is a library for nested, variable-sized data. It’s in the scikit-hep project.

  9. +1614, current rank is 452: jupyter-lsp — Multi-Language Server WebSocket proxy for your Jupyter

I feel like the next time I do this, I need to (1) remove all packages from well-known organizations (2) remove packages on which other popular packages started to depend (3) remove packages which are dependencies of trending newcomers.

Falling Fast

Packages in this category might need support. If you want to become a maintainer, here might be your chance :-)

  1. -3338, current rank is 4255: python-whois — produce parsed WHOIS data for a given domain

Bonus: A small PDF update

I care about the PDF ecosystem, so here is how the packages developed:

pypdf family:

  • pypdf: +163, rank now is 1481 🎉 Maybe we make this pass PyPDF2 this year 🤞

The Python PDF Ecosystem in 2023 Which libraries should you use for which use case?

entry.title: Superstitious beliefs in Software Engineering
entry.summary: The Monkey-Ladder Experiment and what it teaches about “we have always done it like that”
entry.content:
The Monkey-Ladder Experiment is a parable from “Competing for the Future” by Gary Hamel and C. K. Prahalad (1994) and goes like this:

4 monkeys in a room. In the center of the room is a tall pole with a bunch of bananas suspended from the top. One of the four monkeys scampers up the pole and grabs the bananas. Just as he does, he is hit with a torrent of cold water from an overhead shower. He runs like hell back down the pole without the bananas. Eventually, the other three try it with the same outcome. Finally, they just sit and don’t even try again. To hell with the damn bananas. But then, they remove one of the four monkeys and replace him with a new one. The new monkey enters the room, spots the bananas and decides to go for it. Just as he is about to scamper up the pole, the other three reach out and drag him back down. After a while, he gets the message. There is something wrong, bad or evil that happens if you go after those bananas. So, they kept replacing an existing monkey with a new one and each time, none of the new monkeys ever made it to the top. They each got the same message. Don’t climb that pole. None of them knew exactly why they shouldn’t climb the pole, they just knew not to. They all respected the well established precedent. EVEN AFTER THE SHOWER WAS REMOVED! (Source)

It’s well-illustrated on Stack Exchange.

The interesting part of this thought experiment is that the monkeys never learn the rules by which the cold water is triggered.

Without knowledge or understanding of the mechanism, we just repeat what others did. We need to challenge the status quo.

You might hear sentences like this at work (and I might even say it!):

  • “Don’t touch this” [because it’s working / too complex]
  • “We have always done it like that” [but I don’t know why] ⚠️
  • “I don’t know why, but we should do it like this”

The important part is to learn something so that you don’t have to repeat the same mistake multiple times. You can do that in three steps:

  1. Documentation: Document what you’re doing in tickets / issues (e.g. Jira) or in Wiki systems (e.g. Confluence) or public chat channels (e.g. Slack).
  2. Add Context: Give enough context so that it can be repeated.
  3. Add hints for future-you: Give hints when it can be tried again, e.g. a link to an issue ticket (e.g. you might find a ticket to a third-party software bug that needs to be fixed first).

Those were my 2 cents for better software development. Cheers!

entry.title: Always use the latest version, but not instantly
entry.summary: People don’t make security advisories. They might not even explicitly state that there was/is a security issue.
entry.content:
This is a warning to my fellow software developers. I’m writing this article as the current maintainer of pypdf and PyPDF2, probably the most widely used PDF packages in the Python ecosystem. At the same time, I’m working as a lead developer at a FinTech company and was working as a software engineer consultant for several years.

My experience is mainly from the Python ecosystem, but the same ideas are true for any programming language with anonymously developed and shared packages. That especially includes JavaScript, Java, PHP, Ruby, and Rust.

“Always the latest” or “don’t touch running systems”?

Almost all software developers use third-party libraries to create their software systems. It’s necessary. At the same time, I think it’s completely impossible for anybody to review all the code properly. It’s already hard to just check the changelog thoroughly to make sure the updates don’t break anything in your own software.

In that environment, you might be tempted to stick with the “don’t touch running systems” philosophy. You only make an update when it’s absolutely necessary. That means when you need new functionality, when the package you use does not work with other new packages, or when there is a bug or security issue that affects you.

In contrast, the “always use the latest version” philosophy is to always try to update. Try to use the latest version… but not right away. In this article I’ll explain why I strongly suggest going with this.

№ 1: Small updates are less painful than big ones

Software evolves over time. When you make the small updates, you might not even recognize the tiny adjustments you make to your software.

Professional projects like Django have extensive CHANGELOGs and a deprecation process. pypdf has one as well. If you look at the warnings, you will be able to make the change before it breaks stuff. That doesn’t work if you upgrade several major versions at once.

№ 2: Security implications are not always clear

Parsing PDF files is pretty hard as the standard is so big. PDF viewers are not strict about the standard, just like browsers are not strict about the HTML standard either. That raises the expectation of users that PDF libraries also handle broken PDFs gracefully, if possible.

In that context, pypdf had infinite loops a couple of times. If you use them in a script that you execute, it’s not too bad. You just interrupt the script and you’re fine. But if you’re using it on a web server and people can trigger this, it can use your CPU. That raises the risk of a Denial of Service attack and thus breaking Availability.

When I became the maintainer of pypdf, it was not immediately clear to me that an infinite loop would have this implication. Also, what should I do with that knowledge?

Now I know that I need to create a Security Advisory (example): This will let your users know that there is a potentially severe issue. Attackers will also know, but they might also have that knowledge already. The security advisory will also make Dependabot and similar tools trigger an update alert for your users.

№ 3: Mixed updates

There are tons of projects out there which have only one, maybe two regularly contributing open source developers. They don’t have the resources to manage multiple major versions. If there is a known issue, it’s fixed in the latest version. Previous versions might also be affected, but don’t receive an update.

Big projects like Django and Ubuntu have the resources to support multiple versions. Small ones don’t. And even for the big ones I would be a bit suspicious if that always works.

Why I don’t instantly use the latest version

Testing is hard and the test coverage of projects is mixed. For huge projects like Python and Django I typically wait until the first patch-update is out. So I wouldn’t use django==5.0.0, but wait for django==5.0.1.

That way others have stumbled over the issues and the community fixed them before I need to do it. At least on my production systems, I don’t want those surprises. On testing systems or private projects I prefer to take the latest and greatest 😄

entry.title: Arrange-Act-Assert vs Given-When-Then
entry.summary: Or: How to structure your tests
entry.content:
Unit tests typically consist of three meaningful phases:

  • Arrange: Set up the preconditions for the tests. That could be creating data/objects or configuring a state.
  • Act: Perform the action that should get tested. Typically this means calling the function/method you want to test.
  • Assert: Verify the correctness of the outcome. Typically this means comparing the actual return value with the expected return value, but it could also mean to check Exceptions or log messages.

If you make it explicit, you can call this the AAA pattern. But there are a few other names of patterns you might have seen.

Code using that pattern with pytest (Python) looks like this:

def test_foo():
    # Arrange
    bar = generate_bar()
    baz = generate_baz()

    # Act
    actual_result = foo(bar, baz)

    # Assert
    expected_result = "abc"
    assert actual_result == expected_result

Please note: If you need to do the same things again and again in the “arrange” step, you can write pytest fixtures.

The Four-phase test pattern

The four-phase pattern is what you might know from JUnit in Java and unittest in Python.

  • Setup: Prepare the preconditions for the test
  • Exercise: Call the function/method that is tested
  • Verify: Compare the actual output with the expected output
  • Teardown: Clean up

You typically have a class that has the setup / teardown methods as well as a test_xyz method containing both, exercise and verify.

Note that this is almost the same as Arrange-Act-Assert. Only the “teardown” is missing in AAA.

import unittest


class FooTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        # Executed before each test_* method
        self.bar = generate_bar()
        self.baz = generate_baz()

    def tearDown(self):
        # Executed after each test_* method
        self.bar = None
        self.baz = None

    def test_foo(self):
        # Act
        actual_result = foo(self.bar, self.baz)

        # Assert
        expected_result = "abc"
        self.assertEqual(actual_result, expected_result)

Given-When-Then (GWT) in comparison to AAA

In behavior-driven development (BDD) people like to use GWT:

  • Given: Similar to Arrange
  • When: Similar to Act
  • Then: Similar to Assert

GWT describes a scenario from the user’s point of view, while AAA describes the structure of the test code. However, they are essentially the same.

entry.title: The Python PDF Ecosystem in 2023
entry.summary: Which libraries should you use for which use case?
entry.content:
The Python PDF ecosystem is a mess. There are tons of packages on PyPI, but many of them are inactive. As I had the dubious fortune of having to work with PDF documents a couple of times in my career as a Python developer, let me guide you through this jungle.

Although people have all kinds of Python/PDF-related issues, most are around three topics: (1) Read text from PDF documents (2) Read tables from PDF documents (3) Generate PDF documents. I’ll focus on those.

Full disclosure: I am the maintainer of pypdf and PyPDF2. I am biased when it comes to those libraries.

The Top Libraries by PyPI Download Statistics 🏆

The PyPI download statistics from March 2023 (30 days, ending in 2023–03–01 09:13:26):

  • 588. pypdf2, downloaded 4,642,155× — inactive, use pypdf
  • 824. pdfminer-six (SO), downloaded 2,883,693×, used by textract
  • 944. reportlab (SO), downloaded 2,194,928×
  • 1,577. fpdf, downloaded 838,745× — inactive, use fpdf2
  • 1,647. weasyprint (SO), downloaded 764,438×
  • 1,701. pdfkit (SO), downloaded 713,056×
  • 1,810. pdf2image (SO), downloaded 619,182×
  • 1,983. xhtml2pdf (SO), downloaded 506,259× — uses reportlab
  • 2,089. pymupdf (SO), downloaded 450,426×
  • 2,107. pikepdf (SO), downloaded 443,106×
  • 2,350. pdfplumber (SO), downloaded 358,563× — uses pdfminer.six
  • 2,430. pyhanko (SO), downloaded 333,172×
  • 2,599. Apache tika (SO), downloaded 294,887×
  • 2,715. pypdf (SO), downloaded 269,823×
  • 2,835. fpdf2 (SO), downloaded 244,516×
  • 2,839. pypdf3, downloaded 243,892× — inactive, use pypdf
  • 3,260. tabula-py (SO), downloaded 176,789× — wrapper for tabula-java
  • 3,334. pdfrw, downloaded 168,797× — inactive, use pypdf
  • 3,448. pdfminer, downloaded 156,558×, inactive, use pdfminer.six
  • 3,580. sphinxcontrib-svg2pdfconverter, downloaded 144,795×
  • 3,703. img2pdf, downloaded 134,859×
  • 4,242. camelot-py (SO), downloaded 100,638×
  • 4,572. pdfservices-sdk (SO), downloaded 86,805×

PyPI download statistics don’t represent popularity properly. People who have automatic Continuous Integration (CI) systems / build systems download their packages again and again. They easily make it appear as if the package is used all the time. That is an inherent skew towards libraries/frameworks used in web development.

Some projects have Anaconda packages and even Debian / Ubuntu packages. That reduces the number of PyPI downloads.

There are some libraries where the users should obviously migrate:

  • Use pypdf: There is no good reason to use PyPDF2, PyPDF3, PyPDF4 anymore
  • Use pdfminer-six: Why do people still use pdfminer?
  • Use fpdf2: fpdf was last updated in 2018 and doesn’t support Python 3.9.

Text Extraction from PDF Documents 📖

If you simply want to get the complete text of a PDF page, but don’t care about its exact position, my PDF text extraction benchmark shows the best choices:

  • pypdfium2 (Apache-2.0 or BSD-3-Clause license): It’s fast and the text extraction is very good. The only downside might be that it might be hard to install as it relies on PDFium (Apache 2.0 license) which is a C++ project.
  • Apache Tika (Apache-2.0 license) is a little bit slower and a little bit worse in text extraction quality, but still excellent. It is a Java project and the server has to be started, so the first run might be slow.
  • PyMuPDF (GNU AFFERO GPL 3.0 / Commercial), also called “fitz”, is on-par with Tika. It relies on MuPDF by Artifex Software, Inc. under AGPLv3. It’s a C project and thus might come with the same installation issues as pypdfium2 / tika. The commercial license is something you need to check.
  • pypdf (BSD license) is a pure Python project. I became the maintainer of it in April 2022 and since then we could improve its quality a lot. Its text extraction speed is roughly 10x — 20x slower than the one of pypdfium2/tika/PyMuPDF. The text extraction quality is roughly the same, but the other three projects deal better with whitespaces. PyPDF2, PyPDF3, PyPDF4 should no longer be used. They are forks of pypdf which are far behind in development and no longer maintained. Use pypdf.

If you want some extra information, e.g. which font was used for a specific word or where exactly the character is on the page, then use pdfminer.six or pdfplumber (built on pdfminer.six). Their text extraction quality is worse than the one of the other four libraries, though.

Extracting tables is another special case of text extracting. camelot-py, tabula-py, and pdfplumber approach this.

A completely different topic is extracting text from images (or scanned PDF documents). That is OCR. Try tesseract for that task.

Generating PDF Documents 🔨

I see two reasonable choices to create PDF documents:

  1. Create the raw PDF from code: Here reportlab is the only option I have tried so far, but fpdf2 also exists. edit: As the maintainer of pypdf and PyPDF2, I will work more closely with fpdf2 in future. They seem to have a good community and the project seems well-managed!
  2. Create an intermediate format and convert it to PDF: There are several options, e.g. pdfkit or xhtml2pdf (using HTML) or pdflatex (using LaTeX). There are certainly way more, e.g. docx2pdf. I haven’t used those, though.
  3. Images: You can convert SVG to PDF via sphinxcontrib-svg2pdfconverter and other images via img2pdf.

In all cases, you can add metadata with pypdf.

Reading and Writing PDF Metadata 📝

Reading and writing PDF metadata with Python can be done with multiple libraries:

  • pypdf, see the docs on how to read/write PDF metadata
  • PyMuPDF (docs)
  • pikepdf (docs)

Signing a PDF Document

pyhanko is the only option here.

Python PDF Applications 👩💻

  • pdfly: View metadata, create a 2-up booklet, compress a PDF, extract text, and concatenate PDFs.
  • pdfalyzer: In-depth analysis of PDF files

There is so much more 😲

If you go outside of the Python ecosystem there is obviously much more. See the PDF awesomelist:

GitHub - py-pdf/awesome-pdf: A curated list of resources around PDF files A curated list of resources around PDF files KOReader: a document viewer primarily aimed at e-ink readers…

entry.title: Let your computer speak to you
entry.summary:
I recently injured my eye during a hike. Don’t worry, it’ll be fine soon — but it made me think about text-to-speech (TTS) software again. You probably all know the robotic voices that can read text, but are extremely hard to understand:

Martin Thoma · eSpeak NG: "The Awful German …
entry.content:
I recently injured my eye during a hike. Don’t worry, it’ll be fine soon — but it made me think about text-to-speech (TTS) software again. You probably all know the robotic voices that can read text, but are extremely hard to understand:

Martin Thoma · eSpeak NG: "The Awful German Language" by Mark Twain

This article guides you through the process of utilizing an improved text-to-speech system. Here, you will find complete, functional code that can be executed locally, as well as access to scientific publications for a deeper understanding. Audio examples will illustrate the notable advancements made in recent years. Without further ado, let’s delve into the topic at hand!

The Old Stuff: pyttsx3 and eSpeak

After installing the necessary requirements for pyttsx3, you can use the following Python snippet to generate the audio sample from above:

import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pyttsx3 as tts  # pip install pyttsx3==2.90

# Get the data
with open(sys.argv[1]) as fp:
    data = fp.read()
print(data)

engine = tts.init()

# engine.say(data)  # say it directly
engine.save_to_file(data, Path(sys.argv[2]).resolve())  # store to file

engine.runAndWait()

pyttsx3 is just using the eSpeak NG speech synthesizer. It uses formant synthesis. That technique dates back to the 1950s–1980s (e.g. the Klatt synthesizer). eSpeak builds on the “Speak” software by Jonathan Duddington from around 1995.

The Stages of the Text-To-Speech Pipeline

A text-to-speech (TTS) pipeline contains the following steps:

  • Text Analysis: Find sentence boundaries. Part-of-speech tagging (POS tagging) means that every word gets categorized with its word class (noun, verb, adjective, …). This helps to distinguish homographs like wind (blowing air) and wind (turn or twist).
  • Text Normalization: Convert abbreviations like “e.g.” and units like “°C” into their full form.
  • Phonetic Analysis: Generate a sequence of phonemes. Those are similar to letters, but describe sounds. For example, the word “phoneme” would be written as /ˈfoʊniːm/. The wind (blowing air) is /wɪnd/ whereas the wind (turn or twist) is /waɪnd/. The phonetic analysis might simply be a dictionary lookup (e.g. via CMUdict), but if the word is not found it becomes more complex. Then letter-to-sound (LTS) rules kick in.
  • Prosodic Analysis: Figure out what to stress, how the intonation should be, and how the rhythm of the generated speech should be. The ToBI annotation system can be used.
  • Audio Synthesis: The acoustic model typically generates mel-spectrograms as an input for the waveform generation. This is a high-level acoustic representation.
  • Waveform Generation: The vocoder takes the high-level acoustic representation and converts it into a waveform that can be played as sound.

You can see that the first parts — text analysis and normalization — are clearly natural language processing. Waveform generation is rather digital speech processing. And the rest is somewhere in between.

WaveNet: What Google Speech Services are using

The WaveNet paper was published in 2016 by Google (DeepMind), and it drastically improved audio synthesis and waveform generation. The change of approach is to use data to learn how text should sound, whereas formant synthesis uses knowledge and manual analysis to describe how sounds are generated.

Listen for yourself:

Martin Thoma · eSpeak NG: "The Awful German Language" by Mark Twain

You can use Google Text-to-Speech (TTS) to generate it:

import sys

from gtts import gTTS  # pip install gtts

# Get the data
with open(sys.argv[1]) as fp:
    text = fp.read()

# Generate an mp3
tts = gTTS(text=text, lang="en")
filename = "gtts-text.mp3"
tts.save(filename)

The core innovation of WaveNet compared to formant synthesis was to use a machine learning approach — deep neural networks — for generating raw audio waveforms. Please note that there were other breakthroughs between the two methods.

It’s good, but it’s an external service. You might want to actually generate it on your machine so that nobody else can get your data. Additionally, 2016 is already 7 years ago. A lot has happened in ML since.

End-to-End Deep Learning

Deep learning has not only improved waveform generation but also the other parts. To quote from the Tacotron paper:

Tacotron [is] an end-to-end generative text-to-speech model that synthesizes speech directly from characters.

A few other papers in this context are:

  • 2017 (Google): Tacotron and Tacotron 2. Tacotron takes a text sequence and outputs a feature vector sequence that can be given to WaveNet.
  • 2017 (Baidu): Deep Voice 3 is a neural network-based approach for the acoustic model (the audio synthesis) just like Tacotron. Where Tacotron uses a recurrent neural network (RNN), Deep Voice 3 uses an attention-based approach.
  • 2019 (Microsoft): FastSpeech improves the inference speed compared to Deep Voice 3.
  • 2020 (Kakao): Glow-TTS sped up the training method of the neural network.
  • 2021 (KAIST): VITS (Variational Inference with adversarial learning for end-to-end Text-to-Speech) improves the generated audio quality.

Judge VITS for yourself:

Martin Thoma · VITS: "The Awful German Language" by Mark Twain

Thanks to CoquiTTS (web demo) you can now use this as a complete TTS system to generate this on your machine (note: the company Coqui shut down in early 2024; the TTS package is no longer maintained by Coqui, but a community fork exists: idiap/coqui-ai-TTS):

import sys

from TTS.api import TTS  # pip install TTS


def get_text() -> str:
    with open(sys.argv[1]) as fp:
        text = fp.read()
    text = text.replace("”", '"').replace("“", '"')
    return text


def gen(model_name: str, text: str, out_file: str) -> None:
    # Init TTS with the target model name
    tts = TTS(model_name=model_name, progress_bar=False, gpu=False)
    print("#" * 80)
    print(f"model={model_name}")
    print(f"speakers={tts.speakers}")
    print(f"languages={tts.languages}")
    speaker = None
    if tts.speakers is not None:
        speaker = tts.speakers[0]

    # Select language and speaker
    if speaker == "":
        speaker = None
    language = None
    if tts.languages:
        language = "en"

    # Generate it!
    tts.tts_to_file(
        text=text, speaker=speaker, language=language, file_path=out_file
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    model_name = "tts_models/en/ljspeech/vits--neon"
    speaker = ""
    if len(sys.argv) < 3:
        out_file = f"coqui.wav"
    else:
        out_file = sys.argv[2]
    # if you want to see which models are available: TTS.list_models()
    gen(model_name=model_name, text=get_text(), out_file=out_file)

Summary

In this article, you have learned the basics of text-to-speech systems. You have enough entry points to make a deep dive, and you have complete code so that you can play around with existing systems.

Have fun!

Additional Resources

  • German Text-to-Speech: Lots of audio samples for many TTS systems.
  • Andrew Gibiansky: WaveNet and Tacotron aren’t TTS systems, 2020.

entry.title: pypdf: The 2022 Review
entry.summary: Better text extraction, encryption, and project setup
entry.content:
pypdf is a free and open-source pure-python PDF library capable of splitting, merging, cropping, and transforming the pages of PDF files. It can also add custom data, viewing options, and passwords to PDF files. pypdf can retrieve text, images, and metadata from PDFs as well.

The library has quite a history. It started with pyPdf (2005–2010), continued with PyPDF2 (2011–2016), and had PyPDF3 and PyPDF4 (2018–2022).

What did we achieve in 2022?

We had tons of achievements in 2022 for PyPDF2 / pypdf and I’m happy that the community was so active. There were a few categories of improvements that I would like to highlight:

  • The text-extraction capabilities of pypdf were improved by pubpub-zz. According to my PDF text extraction benchmark there is still room for improvement, especially when it comes to whitespace. The rest is pretty solid.
  • The encryption/decryption capabilities of pypdf were improved by exiledkingcc.
  • Project governance was defined, documentation was created, Continuous Integration (CI) was set up, and a lot of tests were written.
  • We moved from PyPDF2 to pypdf again. Now we have a name that is all lowercase and without a number — consistently, everywhere. This makes it easier for beginners to know what to install and what to import. It also makes it easier to identify the main project.
  • A modern library interface: Replacing PdfFileReader with PdfReader, using len(reader.pages) instead of reader.getNumPages(), reader.metadata instead of reader.getDocumentInfo(), …

April 2022 in Numbers

In April 2022, I took over the responsibility of being the PyPDF2 maintainer. The library was already mature: It had a large user base, several other projects that depended on it, the code was working. But the maintainer shifted his focus to other topics in his life. Don’t forget, it’s an unpaid free-time project.

Development Activity:

  • Contributors: 68
  • Forks: 1k

Maintenance:

  • Open PRs: Over 100
  • Open Issues: 321

Community Engagement:

  • Used by: 29.1k
  • Questions on Stack Overflow: 776
  • Watchers: 153
  • Stars: 4.1k

2022 in Numbers

Development Activity and Maintenance:

  • Contributors: 158 (+132%)
  • Forks: 1151 (+15%)
  • PRs: 526 in total, only 10 left open (link)
  • Issues: 205 in total, 47 left open (link)

Community Engagement:

  • Used by: 38054 (+31%)
  • Questions on Stack Overflow: 1235
  • Watchers: 139 (-9%) — I guess there was just too much activity or people were not really interested.
  • Stars: 5005 (+22%)
  • Downloads: 4.2 million last month for PyPDF2 (link) and 47k for pypdf (link). PyPDF3 has 301k and PyPDF4 has 48k last month.

What do we want to achieve in 2023?

We are an open-source project without a big organization behind it. We don’t have paid developers and for that reason, we can’t make a clear roadmap with the features we will deliver.

However, we have a list of moonshot extensions. Those are hard new features that we want to work on eventually.

We also have 14 issues with handling forms. It would be really nice if we could fix some of those.

entry.title: The 6 Levels of Issue Reporting
entry.summary: From Yelling to doing it yourself
entry.content:
Reporting issues is a core competency a lot of people lack. That is unfortunate not only for the companies who have to deal with angry customers who loudly complain but also for those customers because it’s unlikely their problem will get solved.

When I think about issues, it’s from a developer's perspective. I’m thinking of bugs. But you can also think about businesses or public institutions and their processes.

Nº1: It’s broken!

Just telling somebody “it’s broken” is the first step. They learn that you are unhappy, but they are very likely unable to change anything.

The same goes for “me too” comments on issues of open source projects.

Nº2: What did you do?

Reproducibility is a key ingredient for fixing a bug. As a developer, I first try to see the bug myself. If I cannot see the bug myself, there might be another issue that the user didn’t tell me about. Hence it’s crucial to have “steps to reproduce”.

Nº3: What did you expect?

It’s not always clear what the expected behavior is. Try to describe it with other words. Explain a little bit of the context.

Nº4: Create a (failing) unit test

Now this one is already really good. It only applies to open source and can only be done by developers.

Essentially, you give them a way to (1) completely understand what you did and (2) automatically check if it worked.

You don’t need to put the unit test into the codebase — just make sure there is a self-contained snippet that shows what is broken. That snippet should typically raise an exception as long as the issue exists. And it should not raise an exception when the issue is gone.

Nº5: Locating the buggy part of the code

People who can pinpoint the problematic area in the code are amazing! In some cases, that part never worked. In other cases, you’re dealing with regressions: Features that once worked, but stopped working at some point.

Once you have a snippet that shows the error clearly, you can easily spot regressions via git bisect. The workflow is like this:

  1. git bisect start
  2. git bisect good some-hash-or-tag
  3. git bisect bad some-hash-or-tag
  4. Now git will switch the commit to something between the good one and the bad one. You execute the test script against that commit. If things look fine, you enter git bisect good. If the issue exists, you enter git bisect bad. This step is repeated until git tells you which exact commit had the problem.

Nº6: Create a fixing pull request

It’s AMAZING when people fix the stuff on their own 👏 Even better, when they add enough context in the Pull Request (PR) so that the maintainer understands what was done and why it was done.

entry.title: Designing Beautiful Command-Line Applications With Python
entry.summary: Five libraries that make your console beautiful
entry.content:
A lot of people still write their command-line applications with Argparse or even Optparse plus input(). Creating outputs is often done directly with print and formatting strings — which gets really hairy when you want to print tables or have some color/emphasis.

There are five libraries that allow you to do WAY better. I can promise the last two will surprise you — let’s get started!

№1 and 2: Use click or Typer for CLIs

click is a library in the Flask ecosystem for creating non-interactive command-line interfaces. It parses command-line arguments/options but uses decorators in a very clever way to do so. Especially the options for creating subcommands are top-notch.

import click


@click.group()
def app():
    """Awesome app doing awesome things."""


@app.command()
@click.option("--count", default=1, help="How much love you want")
@click.argument("name")
def spread(name, count):
    """Spread the love."""
    for i in range(count):
        print(f"{name} loves you ❤️")


@app.command(name="print")
@click.argument("filepath", metavar="FILE", type=click.Path(exists=True))
@click.option("--show-meta", default=False, is_flag=True)
def print_(filepath, show_meta):
    """Print the file."""
    if show_meta:
        print(f"File path: {filepath}")
        print("-" * 80)
    with open(filepath, "r") as f:
        print(f.read())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app()

which looks like this:

$ python click-example.py --help
Usage: click-example.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

Awesome app doing awesome things.

Options:
  --help  Show this message and exit.

Commands:
  print   Print the file.
  spread  Spread the love.

$ python click-example.py print --help
Usage: click-example.py print [OPTIONS] FILE

Print the file.

Options:
  --show-meta
  --help       Show this message and exit.

Typer is a library in the FastAPI ecosystem and very similar to click. In fact, it uses click under the hood. Typer makes great use of type annotations to allow you to create beautiful command-line interfaces with very little effort.

№3: Use rich for output formatting

Rich is a Python library for rich text and beautiful formatting in the terminal. Its documentation is excellent, so I’ll use pretty much just examples from there.

Progress Bars

import time

from rich.progress import Progress

with Progress() as progress:
    task1 = progress.add_task("[red]Downloading...", total=1000)
    task2 = progress.add_task("[green]Processing...", total=1000)
    task3 = progress.add_task("[cyan]Cooking...", total=1000)

    while not progress.finished:
        progress.update(task1, advance=0.5)
        progress.update(task2, advance=0.3)
        progress.update(task3, advance=0.9)
        time.sleep(0.02)

There is also the basic example:

from rich.progress import track

for step in track(range(100), description="Processing..."):
    do_work(step)

Tables

from rich.console import Console
from rich.table import Table

table = Table(title="Star Wars Movies")

table.add_column("Released", justify="right", style="cyan", no_wrap=True)
table.add_column("Title", style="magenta")
table.add_column("Box Office", justify="right", style="green")

table.add_row(
    "Dec 20, 2019", "Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker", "$952,110,690"
)
table.add_row("May 25, 2018", "Solo: A Star Wars Story", "$393,151,347")
table.add_row(
    "Dec 15, 2017", "Star Wars Ep. V111: The Last Jedi", "$1,332,539,889"
)
table.add_row("Dec 16, 2016", "Rogue One: A Star Wars Story", "$1,332,439,889")

console = Console()
console.print(table)

Syntax Highlighting

Syntax highlighting in the console is AMAZING. Apparently rich.syntax.Syntax uses pygments under the hood, so you can choose between many different syntax highlighting themes.

import typer
from pathlib import Path
from rich.console import Console
from rich.syntax import Syntax


def app(filepath: Path = typer.Option(..., exists=True)):
    """Print a python file."""
    with open(filepath, "r") as f:
        code = f.read()
    syntax = Syntax(code, "python", theme="solarized-dark", line_numbers=True)
    console = Console()
    console.print(syntax)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    typer.run(app)

Trees

from rich.tree import Tree
from rich import print

tree = Tree("Life")

prokaryota = tree.add("Prokaryota")
prokaryota.add("Eubacteria")
prokaryota.add("Archaebacteria")

eukaryota = tree.add("Eukaryota")
eukaryota.add("Protozoa")
eukaryota.add("Chordata")
plantae = eukaryota.add("Plantae")
plantae.add("glaucophytes")
plantae.add("[red]red algae")
plantae.add("[green][bold]green algae")
plantae.add("land plants 🌳")
eukaryota.add("Fungi")
eukaryota.add("Animalia")
print(tree)

Prompts and Confirmations

from rich.prompt import Prompt, Confirm

is_correct = False
while not is_correct:
    name = Prompt.ask("Enter your name", default="Martin")
    is_correct = Confirm.ask(f"Is your name '{name}'?")

age = Prompt.ask(
    "What is your age group",
    choices=["<18", "18-25", "25-35", ">35"],
    default="25-35",
)

print(f"You are {name} and your age is {age}.")

Bonus: Rich in the REPL

If you want pretty printing directly in the Python REPL, try this:

>>> from rich import pretty
>>> pretty.install()
>>> ["Rich and pretty", True]

Rich also provides an inspect function which is excellent to figure out what a given object can do:

>>> from rich import inspect
>>> from rich.color import Color
>>> color = Color.parse("red")
>>> inspect(color, methods=True)

№4: Use textual for TUI applications

Textual is a TUI (Text User Interface) framework for Python. It allows you to interact with mouse movements/clicks, have components that listen to keypresses, re-render parts of the screen. I’ve always thought this was only possible in GUI development. Crazy. I love it.

The following code from the README of textual generates the interactive example from the very top:

from rich.panel import Panel

from textual.app import App
from textual.reactive import Reactive
from textual.widget import Widget


class Hover(Widget):
    mouse_over = Reactive(False)

    def render(self) -> Panel:
        return Panel(
            "Hello [b]World[/b]", style=("on red" if self.mouse_over else "")
        )

    def on_enter(self) -> None:
        self.mouse_over = True

    def on_leave(self) -> None:
        self.mouse_over = False


class HoverApp(App):
    """Demonstrates custom widgets"""

    async def on_mount(self) -> None:
        hovers = (Hover() for _ in range(10))
        await self.view.dock(*hovers, edge="top")


HoverApp.run(log="textual.log")

№5: Graphs in the Terminal

If the capabilities of rich and textual weren’t crazy enough for you, give plotext a shot. plotext plots directly on terminal: the syntax is very similar to matplotlib, it has no dependencies (except for an optional dependency required for image plotting) and can save plots as text or as colored HTML 🤯

import plotext as plt  # <--- this is plotext, not matplotlib!

y = plt.sin()  # sinusoidal signal
plt.scatter(y)
plt.title("Scatter Plot")
plt.show()

How to plot a chart in the terminal? I'm researching ML/Theano and recently came across this script…

Summary

click/typer allows you to create a nice static interface to your application, rich gives you a lot of formatting options like progress bars and tables. If you want to stay on the terminal but get GUI-like features, give textual and plotext a try.

Now that you know how to create nice terminal applications with Python, you should make sure that your terminal is shiny as well:

How to get an amazing Terminal In Windows and Linux; including prompts, fonts, and colors

entry.title: The State of PyPI — 2022 Edition
entry.summary: Let’s see how the Python Package Index evolved in 2022
entry.content:
PyPI, the python package index, is the default package repository for Python. It’s completely open and free to use for anybody. Anybody can contribute packages. PyPI is also the default package index for Python: When you run pip install flake8 the package manager will typically look on PyPI for flake8.

What kind of packages are on PyPI? Continue to find out 😄

Context of this Analysis

It’s the third time that I run such an analysis. The first was in January 2015 (source) and the second one was in January 2020 (source).

Methodology: Data Cleaning

I’ve essentially downloaded the complete data. Well, only the meta-data and the latest package versions. The metadata is about 3.4 GB of data and the latest versions of all packages are around 200 GB of data.

As everybody can upload packages on PyPI, there are a lot of unusable packages.

At the time of this data dump, there were 53,408 packages that classified themselves as Alpha-stage or even earlier. Several hundred packages had “Example Author” or similar in the author field. More than 800 package names contained the string “example”. Almost 2000 packages indicated that the readers were trying an example from a “Head First” book.

A lot of packages never reach a point where they are useful to anybody. Even more are abandoned. I consider a package which isn’t updated for more than a year abandoned. There were over 129k packages which didn’t receive any edit in 2021 or 2022. This includes the PyPDF2 package which is still pretty wide-spread.

All of those packages were removed and ignored in the follow-up analysis. This left 78,950 packages (complete list). For those packages I could imagine that people actually use them.

Ecosystems

There are several ecosystems within Python. It’s typically driven by one application or framework for which many people write extensions/plugins. In fact, there are so many ecosystems that I cannot enumerate them all. Hence I will only present the biggest ones. To be in those, the ecosystem has to have at least 100 packages that belong to it.

Please remember that a huge number of packages typically means that the ecosystem is a bit older, but it can also mean that many important features are missing. I didn’t analyze how mature those packages are or if they are maintained at all.

Web Frameworks

WSGI made it easy to create a web framework in Python. The biggest one for sure is Django (2,757 packages) with the batteries-included philosophy. Microframeworks try to provide the bare minimum. This category contains Flask (548 packages), FastAPI (182 packages), Tornado (50 packages), and Bottle (31 packages).

Plone (398 packages which contain either “collective” or “plone”) is a CMS just like Wagtail (92 packages) or Django-CMS (10 packages).

Dash (34 packages) is a framework for building data apps by plotly. I guess it’s similar to streamlit (57 packages).

Machine Learning and Data Analysis

In the machine learning space, we have ecosystems around the deep learning libraries Torch (735 packages), Keras (135 packages), and Tensorflow (327 packages).

For data analysis, there is Jupyter (850 packages) and Pandas (383 packages).

For robotic process automation (RPA), there is robotframework (108 packages).

As general libraries, there is scikit (202 packages, including sklearn), numpy (248 packages), and scipy (68 packages).

Companies

When a company provides popular services, developers will write supplementary packages to simplify their lives.

For cloud computing, the dominant players are AWS (1,213 AWS/boto packages), Google Cloud Platform (59 packages), and Microsoft Azure (448 packages).

Other packages are around Alibaba (474 packages), Discord (414 packages), Slack (100 packages), and Sentry (62 packages).

Testing

The testing world pretty much consolidated around pytest (386 packages) for writing unit tests, mypy (484 packages) for type checking, and the static linter Flake8 (125 packages).

Tooling

  • over 100 packages contain ‘pip’
  • 231 packages contain ‘redis’
  • 282 packages contain ‘docker’

Tools around data formats

Reading and writing data is a common and cumbersome task. There are several packages that simplify working with SQL (1,116 packages), JSON (1,064 packages), PDF (580 packages), and Markdown (381 packages).

Other

  • Odoo: According to Wikipedia, Odoo is a suite of business management software tools including, for example, CRM, e-commerce, billing, accounting, manufacturing, warehouse, project management, and inventory management. 3,283 packages contain ‘odoo’.
  • AsyncIO: Working in an asynchronous way has a couple of benefits that many people don’t want to miss. However, switching from a synchronous implementation to an asynchronous one is not always that easy. 8313 packages or their descriptions contain “aio” or “asyncio”.
  • MicroPython: Did you know that CPython is only the most common implementation of the Python standard? MicroPython is another one that is tailored towards microcontrollers. There are 47 packages for this Python runtime.

Package Authors

Who creates packages on PyPI?

Sadly, the “author” meta field was not filled out for 3,995 packages. In several cases, it’s also filled with nonsense that indicates that the package should probably not be taken seriously (521x Example Author). Others, like hfpython (473 packages) — Head First — might come from examples from learning material.

There are a couple of organizations that created a lot of packages: Various Odoo Community Associations (combined 4,446 packages), Amazon Web Services (438 packages), Microsoft Corporation (272 packages), and Alibaba Cloud SDK (368 packages).

There are also foundations like OpenStack (260 packages) and The Apache Software Foundation (152 packages). Even single contributors like Vlad Emelianov (307 packages, mostly type stubs for boto3) make notable amounts of packages.

Licenses

One of the pain points of single developers working in their free time on projects is to choose the proper license. It’s not fun. It feels like work. But without having a clear license, it might be impossible for others to use your software.

Many developers did not bother to give any license information (24,299 packages), some refer to a file (2,732). The most common choices are MIT (24,234), APACHE LICENSE 2.0 (7,889), AGPL-3 (4,193), BSD (2,474), GPLv3 (2,751), BSD-3-CLAUSE (1,799). All other licenses are used by fewer than 1000 packages or in too many different spellings.

Big Packages

75% of the packages on PyPI are below 56 KB in size. 95% of the packages on PyPI are below 2,328 KB in size. 99% of the packages on PyPI are less than 27 MB.

You can see that a minority of packages consume most of the space. And the ones above 500 MB are:

  • mxnet-cu102==1.7.0.post0: 895 MB (pypi)
  • torch==1.4.0: 753 MB (pypi)
  • daal-static==2021.2.3: 623 MB (pypi)

The default limit is at 100 MB, but you can ask for more.

Ridiculous Stuff

The longest package name has 122 characters. The same package has the longest release_url (152 characters), the longest package URL (148 characters).

The longest version string has 70 characters, the longest summary is 4570 characters long.

Finally, something that looks serious: The khmer package lists 70 authors in 1105 characters.

Security

Open package repositories such as PyPI (but also Composer in PHP) have a problem with malicious packages and typo squatting.

For PyPI, there are several examples such as jeIlyfish vs jellyfish and python3-dateutil vs dateutil.

It’s hard to estimate how severe that issue is.

I’ve tried to find malware via clamscan, but I only got 45 false-positives (e.g. bgmi, cp-mn-bd-01-mimicat). I’ve checked those tar.gz files via virustotal.

There are several attack vectors:

  • Typosquatting: Your developers want to use jellyfish, but do write jelyfish (just one “l”). While there are no ways to completely prevent it, one can add a link to the GitHub repository and the PyPI package in the README (e.g. as a badge like here). GitHub and its stars/forks allow you to reason at least a little bit easier which one is the correct one.
  • Dependency confusion: You have an internal package bmw-ci. It’s not expected to be on pypi.org, but to be loaded from your internal package repository. However, an angry former employee knows that and uploads his version of that package on pypi. As pip searches first on pypi.org and then in your private repository, the attacker’s package is installed.
  • Trojan horse: You’re installing a package which has some nice functionality, but the author is an attacker.
  • Supply chain attack: You’re making use of the package awesome-foobar and the author is a good guy. However, it’s just a free-time project for that author. The author does not have the time or knowledge to take security seriously. An attacker figures out his password and uploads a new version of the package that contains malware.

And many things that malicious software can do:

  • Data stealing malware: Grab ssh keys, get your crypto wallet keys, get your bank account passwords, log your passwords, send your private photos, …
  • Ransomware: Encrypting your data and demanding a ransom
  • Backdoors: Allowing the attacker to access your computer

A serious issue with PyPI is that you cannot report packages easily (#3896). Update: Since 2024, PyPI has a “Report project as malware” button.

File Names

There are a couple of file names you would expect to appear in most packages: __init__.py, PKG-INFO, setup.py, setup.cfg. Let’s see what else we’ve got:

README

It’s most of the time a README.md. More than 3x the amount of README.rst.

License

Most people prefer LICENSE over LICENSE.txt

Should this be in here?

People ship files that should not be in the package. The most obvious one is .gitignore, but also rendered documentation.

What have we seen?

The Python ecosystem is thriving with several thousands of actively developed packages. It’s a mix of single contributors, open organizations, and corporations who contribute.

PyPI contains a lot of packages for data science and web development, but also security tools.

entry.title: 5 Ways to get Enums in Python
entry.summary: There should be one — and preferably only one — obvious way to do it.
entry.content:
An Enum is a collection of static values, typically strings or integers. They are used pretty often — or at least they should be. At Cashlink, we typically use them to track steps for longer processes.

Enums are a way to group constants. Constants are useful to prevent typos as your editor can warn you when a value is not part of an enum, but it cannot warn you that a string or an integer is invalid. Grouping constants in Enums gives you a couple of advantages.

Before we dive into it, let’s look at some applications for enums.

Examples of Enums

  • Statuses: You’re writing a backend and you want to return a status code, this should be an enum. Instead of writing return 404 you write return status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND. In general, variables that contain a finite set of statuses should probably have an Enum as value. Look for “state” or “status”.
  • Choices: It might be salutations a user can choose from or roles of users. Countries of origin, timezones, …. Look for “choice” or sometimes just lists within your code.
  • Types: You could have different types of users, subscriptions, products, …
  • Steps: If you track the user funnel you might have a constant for each step. Depending on that you could have different behavior. The set of all steps could be an Enum.
  • Flags: The Unix permission system which represents Read / Write / Execute as binary flags in a 3-bit sequence is another example of what you would want to do with an Enum.

What you want to do with enums

Get editor support

You can always just use a constant. But when you use an editor, you typically want to get auto-completion by your editor.

Nice representation when printing
