There should be a good way to convert it to a string. For example, when you print the HTTP status code I think NOT_FOUND is way better than 404.

Iterate over all values

An enum is a collection of static values. In some cases, you want to loop over all of them.

Exhaustiveness Checks

In a lot of codebases you can see this pattern:

if value == 'a':
    ...
elif value == 'b':
    ...
elif value == 'c':
    ...
else:
    # Safeguard if a case was forgotten
    raise NotImplementedError(f"The value {value} should not exist")

I’ve also seen ValueError for exactly the same thing.

Depending on where those values come from, you could compare value against an enum. Then mypy could do an exhaustiveness check, meaning it will understand that there is the possibility to run into the exception. Hence mypy can warn you that you actually forgot a case!

Semantically meaningful comparisons

Comparing values is easy, but comparing semantics is hard. We want to compare things of the same kind, not values. For example, we want to compare if a payment we received is equal to the amount we expected. It has to be in the same unit. It makes a huge difference if we expect 1000 Euro or 1000 Indonesian Rupiah. It also makes a huge difference for some people if you speak of biological sex or gender identity. This means that two variables might contain exactly the same value, but not be comparable. At the very least we would expect a comparison to evaluate to False.

Serialization and Deserialization

We need to convert data so often to JSON and back from JSON. Pydantic is pretty amazing and does a great job coercing to the right values most of the time, but let’s check for the given options how well they do.

№ 1: The built-in Enum module

The enum module was introduced with Python 3.4 via PEP 435. It is the first thing that should pop to your mind when you want to create an Enum:

from enum import Enum


class HttpStatus(Enum):
    NOT_FOUND = 404
    SUCCESS = 200
    INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR = 500

# Printing
>>> print(HttpStatus.SUCCESS)
HttpStatus.SUCCESS

# Comparisons
>>> HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND == 404
False

>>> HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND.value == 404
True

# Iteration
>>> for value in HttpStatus:
...     print(value)
HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND
HttpStatus.SUCCESS
HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR

Integer Flags can be done with IntFlag.

If you want to check for exhaustiveness, you can get this:

from typing import NoReturn


def assert_never(value: NoReturn) -> NoReturn:
    assert False, f"Unhandled value: {value} ({type(value).__name__})"


def print_status(status: HttpStatus) -> None:
    if status is HttpStatus.SUCCESS:
        print("SUCCESS")
    elif status is HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND:
        print("NOT_FOUND")
    else:
        assert_never(status)

Which gives you this error message:

$ mypy main.py
main.py:35: error: Argument 1 to "assert_never" has incompatible type "Literal[HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR]"; expected "NoReturn"

You can make Enums JSON-serializable, but you have to give it a little bit of thought:

Convert a Python Enum to JSON A trivial way to make a Python Enum which is based on string tokens JSON-serializable is to inherit both str and Enum…py.watch

№ 2: Plain class attributes

You can simply create a class and use its attributes:

class HttpStatus:
    NOT_FOUND = 404
    SUCCESS = 200
    INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR = 500

# Printing
>>> print(HttpStatus.SUCCESS)
200

# Comparisons
>>> HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND == 404
True

While something like this is still common in many codebases, the downsides are clear:

  1. Value comparisons with other enums lead to unexpected results.
  2. It’s way harder to iterate over the values.
  3. The string representations are just the values that can be hard to read.

№ 3: Constants in a module

You can put the values directly in a module, e.g. http_status_codes.py:

NOT_FOUND = 404
SUCCESS = 200
INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR = 500

This is probably the most lightweight option. You still have all of the disadvantages.

One real-life example where this is done is the Django REST framework with the HTTP status codes (source).

№ 4: Django models.Choices

Django has also several ways to create enums, e.g. TextChoices:

from django.db import models


class HttpStatus(models.TextChoices):
    NOT_FOUND = 404
    SUCCESS = 200
    INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR = 500

# Iteration
>>> for value in HttpStatus:
...     print(value)
404
200
500

# Comparisons
>>> HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND.value == "404"
True
>>> HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND == "404"
True
>>> HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND.value <= "404"
True

# Custom functions
>>> HttpStatus.choices
[('404', 'Not Found'), ('200', 'Success'), ('500', 'Internal Server Error')]
>>> HttpStatus.names
['NOT_FOUND', 'SUCCESS', 'INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR']
>>> HttpStatus.labels
['Not Found', 'Success', 'Internal Server Error']
>>> HttpStatus.values
['404', '200', '500']

There is also models.Choices and models.IntegerChoices.

Django TextChoices Enums add a couple of functions that might come in handy. I’d recommend using them if you use Django. They can be connected to the Django ORM which is pretty nice.

The Django Choices are also directly JSON-serializable.

№ 5: typing.Literal

The Literal type was introduced in PEP 586 as a way to indicate that a variable must have a set of certain values. For example, instead of just stating that a parameter is an integer, you can list the allowed values:

from typing import Literal

StatusCode = Literal[404, 200, 500]

def set_status(self, http_status_code: StatusCode):
    self.status = http_status_code

Now … which one should I take?

First, make sure the type of Enum fulfills your needs:

There are also some other choices:

  • Do you need to support Python 3.3 or earlier? Then you cannot choose enum.Enum.
  • Do you only want to give mypy better capabilities of checking issues? Use typing.Literal!
  • Do you use Django? Then Django Choices are your way to go!

entry.title: Risks and Benefits of The 9 Popular Software Design Principles
entry.summary: Improve your software engineering skills
entry.content:
Every software developer with a little bit of experience knows that keeping things simple and stupid (KISS) makes sense. Once you have learned to use classes and functions, you don’t want to repeat yourself — keep things DRY.

The goal of all of those principles is to make software easy to maintain by reducing mental complexity.

№1: Don’t repeat yourself (DRY)

DRY is the core of software development. We structure our code in packages and modules. We factor out functions. We try to make the code reusable so that we hopefully have an easier time maintaining it.

Benefit: Complexity reduction. The more code you have, the more you need to maintain. DRY typically leads to less code. This especially means that you only need to adjust one place for typical changes.

Risk: If you do it too much, the code typically gets more complex.

Tooling support: There are programs to find duplicated code. For Python, there is pylint --disable=all --enable=similarities src

№2: You Ain’t Gonna Need It (YAGNI)

YAGNI is the realization that too much abstraction actually harms maintainability. Java devs, I’m looking at you!

Benefit: Complexity reduction. Removing abstractions makes it clearer how the code works.

Risk: If you apply YAGNI too much and thus make too few abstractions, you will have a hard time extending your software. And junior devs might mess with the code in a bad way.

Tooling support: None (maybe one could count references to classes throughout the codebase?)

№3: Keep it Simple and Stupid (KISS)

KISS can apply to many situations. Although some solutions are smart and solve the issue at hand, the dumber solution might be better because there is less potential to introduce issues. This might be less DRY from time to time.

№4: Principle of Least Surprise

Design your systems in such a way that the location of a feature implementation as well as the behavior and the side-effects of a component are least surprising. Keep your colleagues in the loop.

Benefit: Complexity reduction. You make sure that the mental model of the system fits what people assume naturally.

Risk: You might need to violate DRY to get this done.

Tooling support: None. However, there are some signs that this was violated: (1) You are explaining the same quirks of your system again and again to new colleagues (2) You need to look the same topic up again and again (3) You feel the need to document a topic that is not inherently complicated.

№5: Separation of Concerns (SoC)

Every package, module, class, or function should only bother about one concern. If you do too many things, you do none of them well.

It is most clear to me in practice in the separation of a data storage layer, a presentation layer, and a layer that contains the business logic. Other types of concerns might be input validation, data synchronization, authentication, …

To phrase it with the Unix philosophy: Do one thing and do it well.

Benefit: Complexity reduction: (1) It’s typically more clear where adjustments need to be done. (2) You should have fewer undesired side-effects you need to think about. (3) People can work in parallel without having crazy many merge conflicts.

Risk: If you go too crazy on SoC, you will likely violate KISS or YAGNI.

Tooling support: You can measure cohesion by counting how many classes/functions from other packages are used. A high number of externally imported functions can indicate violations in SoC. A high number of merge conflicts might also indicate an issue.

№6: Fail early, fail loud

As developers, we have to deal with all kinds of errors. And especially for beginners, it’s not clear how to deal with them.

One pattern that has helped me a lot in the past is to fail early. Meaning very close to the location where the error can happen, the error should be recognized. Especially user input should be validated directly in the input layer. But also network interactions are a common case where you need to handle error cases.

The other pattern is to fail loud, meaning to throw an exception and create a log message. Don’t just return None / NULL. Exceptions are the way to go. Depending on the kind of Exception, you might also want to let the user know.

Benefit: Easier maintainability as it’s clearer where functionality belongs and how the system should be designed. Easier debuggability as errors happen early.

Risk: None.

Tooling support: None

№7: Defensive Programming

Defensive programming is named after defensive driving. Defensive driving is “driving to save lives, time, and money, in spite of the conditions around you and the actions of others”. Defensive programming is the idea to be robust and correct, in spite of the conditions of the environment and the actions of others. This can mean to be robust against wrong input, e.g. when you have an IBAN field in the database to actually make sure that the content being stored there contains an IBAN. It can also mean to make assertions explicit and raise exceptions if those are violated. It can mean to make calls to APIs idempotent. It can mean to have a high test coverage to be defensive against future breaking changes.

Three core rules of defensive programming:

  • All data is important until proven otherwise.
  • All data is tainted until proven otherwise.
  • All code is insecure until proven otherwise.

The alternative to defensive programming is “shit in, shit out”.

Benefit: Higher robustness

Risk: Higher maintenance due to more complex/lengthy code base

Tooling support: Test coverage to see how much your unit tests cover. If you want to go crazy, try mutation testing. For infrastructure, there is chaos engineering. Load testing.

№8: SOLID

The SOLID principles give guidance around coupling and cohesion. They are originally formulated around object-oriented programming (OOP), but you can apply them to different abstraction levels than classes as well, e.g. services or functions. I will just call those “components” later on.

Two components can be coupled in several ways. For example, one service might need knowledge of how another service internally operates to do its work. The stronger component A depends on component B, the stronger A is coupled with B. Please note that this is a symmetric relationship. For coupling, we don’t care about the direction.

A high cohesion of one module means that its internal parts are strongly connected. They all deal with the same topic.

Loose coupling and high cohesion between components is what we strive for.

Single-responsibility principle

“There should never be more than one reason for a class to change.”

The responsibilities of software entities like services, packages, modules, classes, and functions should be clear. They should typically operate on one abstraction level and not do too many things.

The single-responsibility is one of the tools to achieve separation of concerns.

Tooling support: I’m not aware of automatic tools to find violations of the single responsibility principle. However, you can try to describe the functionality of the components without the words “and” / “or”. If this does not work, you might violate it.

Open–closed principle

“Software entities … should be open for extension, but closed for modification.”

If you change a component on which others rely, you are potentially breaking their code.

Liskov substitution principle

“Functions that use pointers or references to base classes must be able to use objects of derived classes without knowing it.”

Benefit: This is a very basic assumption you make in OOP. Just follow it.

Risk: None?

Interface segregation principle

“Many client-specific interfaces are better than one general-purpose interface.”

Benefit: It’s easier to extend the software and reuse interfaces if you can pick and choose. However, if the software is completely in-house, I would rather create bigger interfaces and split once it becomes necessary.

Risk: Violation of KISS / YAGNI.

Dependency inversion principle

“Depend upon abstractions, [not] concretions.”

In some cases, you want to operate on a more general class of inputs than the one specific type you’re currently dealing with. Examples that pop to my mind are WSGI (connecting web servers with web applications), JDBC (database connections), and basically any plugin system (e.g. Flake8). You want to define an interface and depend on that. This interface has then to be implemented by the components.

Assume you have an application that needs to have access to a relational database. You could now implement all queries for all kinds of relational databases. Or you define that the function receives a database connector that implements the JDBC interface. Now the connector has to be extended and not all functions that need the DB connection. That is the inversion.

Benefit: In the long run, this makes the software much easier to maintain as it becomes clearer where functionality lies. It also helps with KISS.

Risk: If you overdo it, you might violate KISS. A rule of thumb would be that at least two classes should implement an interface before you create an interface.

№9: Locality Principle

Don’t separate things that belong together. If two parts of code are typically edited together, try to keep them as close as possible. At least in the same package, hopefully in the same directory, maybe in the same file — and if you’re lucky they can be in the same class / directly below each other within the file.

Benefit: Hopefully fewer merge conflicts. You don’t need to switch context when you try to find that other file. When you refactor that piece, you might remember all things that belong to it.

Risk: Violating loose coupling or separation of concerns.

Tooling support: None so far, but I’m thinking about creating one for Python. Basically, I would analyze the git commits.

Summarizing it: The Zen of Python

I absolutely love the Zen of Python. While it is less concrete than several other principles, it is a piece of programming philosophy that is super important:

Beautiful is better than ugly. Explicit is better than implicit. Simple is better than complex. Complex is better than complicated.

Flat is better than nested. Sparse is better than dense. Readability counts.

Special cases aren’t special enough to break the rules. Although practicality beats purity.

Errors should never pass silently. Unless explicitly silenced.

In the face of ambiguity, refuse the temptation to guess. There should be one– and preferably only one –obvious way to do it. Although that way may not be obvious at first unless you’re Dutch.

Now is better than never. Although never is often better than right now.

If the implementation is hard to explain, it’s a bad idea. If the implementation is easy to explain, it may be a good idea.

Namespaces are one honking great idea — let’s do more of those!

entry.title: The Software Engineering Career Ladder 📈
entry.summary: It only starts at Junior vs Senior
entry.content:
The job market for Software Engineers is crazy at the moment — if you happen to be skilled, you can have your dream job.

In this article, I want to shed some light on one aspect that is relevant when you consider which job to take: The Career Ladder.

When you continue reading the following, please keep in mind that this is mostly a big-tech topic. It doesn’t really apply to startups.

Why does the career ladder matter for an employee?

The level you get rated at for your current job can influence your chances in the next job interviews. Yes, titles are different from company to company. And yes, in some it is easier than in others to get such a title.

The title can also be strongly connected to the compensation you receive and to the types of skills or behavior which are expected from you.

Why does the career ladder matter for employers?

Think about which type of employee you want. Do you want somebody to be constantly working on improving themselves? Do you want an employee who is eager to reach goals?

A clearly formulated and accessible career ladder can help those people to understand what they want to reach. Especially for young employees, this can be encouraging as they might not have their dream salary or position yet. Few things are more frustrating than knowing that you will be locked in your current situation, having the same responsibilities until you retire.

If you have an open position, you have to be clear what you need. Having a career ladder makes it simpler to formulate what you want.

Roles, Titles, and Levels

People get hired for a role. Typical roles in software engineering are Backend Developer, Frontend Developer, Mobile Dev, Machine Learning Engineer, Data Engineer, Data Scientist, Scrum Master, Product Manager, …

While roles describe the area in which you work, titles and levels describe how experienced you are. The titles are names like “junior” and “senior” which are used across companies. The levels are more fine-grained and only used internally. For example, the levels at Microsoft start at 59 and go up to 90. At Facebook, you have E3 to E8.

This article is about job titles in software engineering.

The individual contributor career levels

There are three typical individual contributor career levels:

Junior Engineers have a really hard time making projects from start to finish. They lack important knowledge and need support.

Engineers, let’s call them “mid-level” for easier recognition, can start and finish small projects. I expect that a Junior Engineer can become a mid-level Engineer within 6 months if he is determined and has a good Senior leading him.

Senior Engineers can draft bigger projects from start to end. They have an understanding of which roles are required for a software project. They are not only experts in their specific field (e.g. backend, frontend, mobile, machine learning, data engineering, graphics, …), but they also have some knowledge of adjacent fields. For example, I expect a senior machine learning engineer to have a slight idea of data engineering. Senior engineers can take over the responsibility for a service — that means they can push for refactoring if it becomes hard to maintain. They make sure enough logging / alerting is there for things to run smoothly / be debuggable. Senior Engineers keep improving their knowledge in their field of expertise. They also spread that knowledge to other engineers in the same team.

The tech leadership career levels

While the junior / mid-level / senior levels make sense for every company, the leadership career levels might not exist for smaller companies.

Staff engineers are senior engineers on steroids. Not only do they have their own specific project in mind, but they also know the projects of other teams and are able to align the tech stack and development across teams. They create a good atmosphere in their team. They are role models for others. They can take responsibility not only for a single feature or service but for an entire product.

Principal engineers have a company-wide perspective. They might suggest new products or change the scope of a product. They work closely with company leadership. They have a good grasp of which roles/levels are necessary to hire. They are more on the strategic side and less involved with day-to-day coding.

The next two levels might as well be in the individual contributor track. Both of them recognize the extraordinary abilities of the person.

A distinguished engineer is recognized by their company as being extremely competent in their professional field. I see this less as a level you get hired at, but more as a reward and a recognition of the capabilities. It has to be earned over many years leading to overall outstanding contributions.

Fellow Engineers take it up a notch. They are typically worldwide famous. Those are people who have Wikipedia pages and are recognized for their public contributions. Examples are:

  • Jeff Dean (Wikipedia, Google Fellow): Leads Google AI, played an important role in MapReduce, was part of designing and implementing BigTable and LevelDB.
  • Jim Gray (Wikipedia, Microsoft Fellow): Manager of the Bay Area Research Center, defined the transaction properties that became known as ACID, received the Turing Award in 1998 for contributions to database and transaction processing
  • Don Norman (Wikipedia, Apple Fellow): Director of The Design Lab, author of The Design of Everyday Things, Professor Emeritus of Cognitive Science at the University of California

There are not that many corporate fellows.

The People-Leadership Career Levels

Where the individual contributor career track focuses on technical skills and their impact on the organization, the people-leadership career track is more centered around organization.

The three levels I want to focus on are Engineering Managers (EMs), Engineering Directors, and Vice President of Engineering. James Stanier wrote an excellent article “VP, Director, what?” in which he shows that essentially the number of people being managed and the time-frame over which they plan grows.

While I don’t have direct experience with this role, just think about how many people are in a good tech team. I would say something like 5 to 15 people. The 15 is just my gut feeling — I just have a hard time keeping even remotely track of what more than 15 people do. If you have more than those 15, it’s just hard to get work done. So if you have 30 people, I would expect at least 2 teams. The two team leads can talk with each other; no need for a manager.

Once more than 3 people need to align, you need a manager again. At maximum that manager can have 15 teams. Meaning when you have 15 teams at 15 people each, you need one manager for that. This manager would have 225 people below her/him.

Engineering Managers take care of performance reviews and set levels (sources: Clément Mihailescu, Lena Reinhard). EMs still deal with the day-to-day topics like having 1-on-1s. I would expect an EM to have a team of at least 5, at most 15 people. In my opinion, the time frame over which they must plan is quarterly or maybe in half-years.

Engineering Directors start to manage other managers. I would expect at least 3 teams, at most 15.

A Vice President of Engineering is the next level in this hierarchy. I would expect at least 2 engineering directors and at most 15 below the VP.

Let’s calculate how many people could be below a VP:

15 directors · 15 EMs/director · 15 people/EM = 3375 people

Please be aware that it does not have to be a super strict hierarchy. It might be that there is a EM reporting directly to the VP.

Some organizations are way bigger than that. For example, Alphabet (Google) has 135,301 employees. One of their products, YouTube, already has 7500 employees. This means you definitely need some more layers in between. The solution is to add some “senior” titles, e.g. “senior director of engineering”. Each new level gives you another factor of 15.

However, I think 15 is rather a maximum. It should probably better be 7. That would mean an EM would have 7 people below them, a director would have 49, a VP would have 343 people.

Depending on how many people are below a certain position, you need to have longer time frames in mind when you plan. For example, if you drop a feature set on which several dozens of engineers work you need to have an idea what they should do in future. If you want to expand into a different direction, you might need to hire a completely new team.

Team Lead and Tech Lead

Team Lead and Tech Lead are roles, not levels.

The responsibility of a tech lead is to help team members with technical aspects of their job: Explain the overall architecture, help to debug hard problems, take decisions over the overall architecture, lead technical discussions and decisions. They are in some aspects close to the role of a software architect. Tech leads assure that the code quality is good.

The responsibility of a team lead is to lead the team with respect to human needs: Make sure people feel well in the team, discuss their professional goals. They typically have 1-to-1s with the team members. Mentoring / coaching are parts of a team lead’s tasks.

See also

  • progression.fyi collects career ladders of many tech companies
  • levels.fyi gives you insights into the different names of career levels and the salaries at big tech companies

entry.title: 9 Clean Code Patterns I wish I knew earlier
entry.summary:
Do you know the feeling when you look back at code which you wrote early in your career? I always feel a bit horrified. But there is a positive side to it: I learned something new 😄

A core part of good software is readability. Keeping the mental complexity low so …
entry.content:
Do you know the feeling when you look back at code which you wrote early in your career? I always feel a bit horrified. But there is a positive side to it: I learned something new 😄

A core part of good software is readability. Keeping the mental complexity low so that everybody (including the author) has an easy time understanding it. Clean code patterns help to do so.

In this article, you will get to know 9 clean code patterns that make code easier to read. Please see such patterns as tools. They don’t apply all the time. Don’t get religious about them. The language I use is Python, but the patterns apply outside of Python as well. Let’s start!

№1: Explanatory Variables

This is probably the simplest trick which you can easily apply. If something is hard to understand and you need a comment for it, try giving it a name.

# Bad
if not (
    string.startswith('"""')
    and string.endswith('"""')
    and '"' not in string[3:-3]
):
    return string

# Good
is_triple_quoted_string = string.startswith('"""') and string.endswith('"""')
if not (is_triple_quoted_string and '"' not in string[3:-3]):
    return string

This applies mostly to boolean expressions, but also to regular expressions, and sometimes to return values.

№2: Follow Conventions and Style Guides

Every programming language has a syntax that you need to follow, otherwise, it will not work. And then there are conventions. You don’t have to follow them; it will still work. However, it makes the life of others way easier if you do follow them.

One of the simplest conventions is style guides. In Python it’s PEP 8, Google published guides for C++ / Java, the Oracle Java Code Conventions, in PHP there is PSR-1, …

Other guides are implicit. For example, how a Django project is structured. Where you typically store views, models, and templates.

Find the style guide(s) that are relevant for you and follow them.

Typically, there are also linters or static code analysis tools that help you to get used to the guides. For example, in Python, there is flake8 with a lot of plugins. For the simplest part, the formatting, you can use tools that do it for you. A code autoformatter for Python which I love is black.

№3: Type Checking

I love type annotations in Python. They are optional, but I highly recommend using them. There are also differences in how to use them.

For example, if you have Dict[str, Any] you might want to consider using NamedTuple / TypedDict / pydantic / dataclasses instead.

In some cases, when you use str as the type you might want to consider using NewType to denote which kind of string you are using. Is it an AuthorId? Is it a UserId?

Those two patterns apply to other languages as well. Let’s phrase it like this:

Make good use of the type system.

If you want to know more about type annotations in Python, please read: Type Annotations in Python 3.8 Learn how to make Python code easier to read and less error-prone by gradual typing

If you want to know about the most recent improvements, read my Python 3.10 article.

№4: Consistent Terminology

I work at the FinTech company Cashlink as a Python backend developer. We handle digital securities, e.g. tokens that represent a real value like a part of a solar farm. Those tokens can be transferred. And here it starts to become interesting. Depending on the type of transfer, we must do different things. Either because of regulations or because of technical reasons. So we started to name different types of transfers differently to not be confused all the time:

  • Transfer: Any action that changes a balance. All terms below are some kind of transfer (although I would hesitate to call minting and burning a transfer).
  • Minting: The tokens are generated. This happens first.
  • Issuance: The transfer from the issuer to the investor. This happens second.
  • Move: A transfer from wallet A to wallet B, where A and B belong to the same investor.
  • Handover: A transfer from wallet A to wallet B, where A and B belong to different investors.
  • Burn: Removing tokens from an investor's account.

Those things are important, but there are other examples where the terminology can be different. For example, internal product names and external ones. Marketing might have different needs than development. Try to get a vocabulary that fits most of the company.

№5: Meaningful Names

Think of your codebase like a book. The book has many, many different storylines. The variables are the characters. You can rely a bit on the context, but readers will be confused if you call everybody just “the friend”. They will be annoyed if they need to read half a page just for the name.

  • Avoid too short names like i or x. They are hard to search for. If you write a mathematical function, they might make sense, though.
  • Avoid too long names like InternalFrameInternalFrameTitlePaneInternalFrameTitlePaneMaximizeButtonWindowNotFocusedState. Java developers regularly fall into this trap. Yes, the name might be super exact. However, it makes all the logic around it super hard to understand. There is a nice middle ground between x and InternalFrameInternalFrameTitlePaneInternalFrameTitlePaneMaximizeButtonWindowNotFocusedState.
  • Be consistent with the vocabulary from №4. Also in spelling. Decide if you want to use American English or British English. Decide if you want to write display/show/present/print in your codebase.
  • Avoid data structures in names like user_dict. If you need that, it might be that you’re violating №6. Try to use only one representation of one object. But keep in mind that this is a general rule. It does make sense sometimes to use user_dict.
  • Make use of context. For example, the java.sql.SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException could simply be a java.sql.IntegrityError. Within the sql package, everything should be about SQL. And a ConstraintViolation simply is an Error.

A pattern I like when iterating is to use the plural form for the iterable (ending in “s”) and the singular for the element (without the final “s”):

# Bad
for tmp in users:
    ...

# Good
for user in registered_users:
    ...

By the way: Please share if you’ve seen funny variable naming in the wild 😄

№6: The step-down rule

Keeping a function at one abstraction level helps you to focus on one topic.

Separate logic ↔ data collection/transfer ↔ presentation.

The presentation does not necessarily have to be visual. It can be print statements or it could be an API response.

Marek Hudyma gives a good example of the step-down rule.

In Python, you can sometimes see this when there is a lot of indentation.

№7: Remove Dead Code

Code that isn’t there is code that cannot break. It’s code that will not cause security issues. It’s code that doesn’t need to be maintained. Instead of commenting code out, remove it.

You can use vulture and flake8-eradicate to find such pieces in a Python codebase.

I know the feeling when you have stuff that might be necessary later. I typically try to write a really thorough commit message, removing only those comments/files to be able to find it later if I need it. But there is YAGNI: You aren’t gonna need it!

№8: Use containers

If you pass the same few values around in several places of your codebase you might want to consider writing a container. That could be a class, in Python you can use a dataclass, a NamedTuple, or a TypedDict. If you need to serialize it, a Pydantic class is pretty nice as well.

A prime example where you should likely use a container format is configuration.

№9: Avoid Surprises

This is a no-brainer, but it is sometimes easy to forget. One core part is to avoid side effects. It should be clear whether a function changes state. Another part is to document hacks. Sometimes it is necessary to have hacks, but at least leave a comment on why the hack is there.

Don’t try to do something smart. Follow the KISS principle — Keep it simple, stupid!

Summary

Writing good code is like writing good articles: It needs practice and you will always improve. Read a lot, ask for feedback and encourage people to also give small little notes in feedback. The ones that don’t matter too much, but are just personal preferences.

Finally, understand what you hate when you read code. Avoid those patterns 😄 — but apply this 😍 Practice, be open to feedback, look critically at your code. Then you will be an awesome software engineer 🥂

entry.title: How Concurrency can Break your Software
entry.summary: Race conditions related to insufficient transaction isolation
entry.content:
We have seen phenomenal improvements in the hardware in the last 30 years. Moore observed that the number of transistors in a dense integrated circuit (IC) doubles roughly every two years, the CPU clock rate increased from 740 kHz in 1970 to 4.9 GHz in 2021, and the types of instructions CPUs can execute got more complex over time. But there are limits to increasing the clock rate and adding more complex instructions. Instead of doing that, CPU manufacturers added the possibility to execute more stuff concurrently. This comes with its own set of problems.

To me, the most interesting ones are in the context of web services. Most prominently, they are interactions with a central database and are related to transaction isolation. In this article, you will learn what the best-known problems of missing isolation are and which transaction isolation levels fix them. Let’s start!

The Basics 📚

Databases organize multiple operations in transactions. You can imagine a database as a sequence of transactions. If a transaction is part of the database, we say it is committed. If a transaction fails, a rollback is executed. The transaction is undone.

We want transactions to be atomic — either a transaction is completely part of the database or not at all. There should not be a partially committed transaction.

We also want transaction isolation — concurrent executions of transactions don’t lead to different results than serial executions. It should not matter if transactions are executed one after each other or in parallel.

The problems we will investigate in this article are called read phenomena and they occur when the isolation property is broken. Having stronger isolation comes at a cost. The tradeoff is speed versus guarantees that certain problems don’t occur. These guarantees are called transaction isolation levels. Controlling the issues is also called concurrency control. There is optimistic and pessimistic concurrency control. Optimistic concurrency control uses snapshot and validation, pessimistic concurrency control uses locks. It’s called optimistic because it first allows changes to happen and rolls back if necessary. It assumes things will be fine, whereas locks assume that something will go wrong. Depending on what happens more often, it’s cheaper to be optimistic or pessimistic.

Do it Yourself! 🔨

If you want to execute the following statements, you need PostgreSQL running:

$ sudo su - postgres
$ psql
# CREATE TABLE balances (id varchar PRIMARY KEY, balance int);
CREATE TABLE

# INSERT INTO balances (id, balance) VALUES ('Alice', 500), ('Bob', 500);
INSERT 0 2

# SELECT * FROM balances;

id   | balance
-------+---------
Alice |     500
Bob   |     500

Dirty Reads: Reading uncommitted data

When transaction T2 sees a non-committed transaction T1, it’s called a dirty read.

Imagine this scenario: Alice and Bob are in a relationship. Alice is good at bookkeeping and keeps track of the financial situation, whereas Bob is sometimes not that financially responsible. In this case, he wants to buy a fantasy sword for 600 €. Luckily, their bank rejects transactions if the balance would drop below 0 €. But Alice checks Bob's account in between.

So we have two transactions:

  • T1: Bob tries to pay for the fantasy sword, which fails and gets rolled back.
  • T2: Alice checks the account.

To execute a transaction to another bank, the bank of Alice and Bob runs the following transfer_out function:

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION
    transfer_out(source VARCHAR, amount INT) RETURNS void AS $$
DECLARE
    source_balance_after int;
BEGIN
    UPDATE balances SET balance = balance - amount WHERE id = source;
    SELECT balance FROM balances WHERE id = source INTO source_balance_after;
    IF source_balance_after < 0 THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'Account % does not have enough money', source;
    END IF;
END
$$
LANGUAGE 'plpgsql' ;

Both initially have 500 EUR on their accounts each.

-- T1: Bob tries to get that fantasy sword
BEGIN TRANSACTION
    -- Step 1: Pay for the sword
    UPDATE balances SET balance = balance - 600 WHERE id = 'Bob';

    -- Step 2: Check if the balance got negative (it did: rollback)
    SELECT balance FROM balances WHERE id = 'Bob';
END TRANSACTION

-- T2: Alice checks the accounts
BEGIN TRANSACTION
    -- Step 1: Read the balance of Bob's account
    SELECT balance FROM balances WHERE id = 'Bob';

    -- Step 2: Read the balance of Alice's account
    SELECT balance FROM balances WHERE id = 'Alice';
END TRANSACTION

As we have two transactions, those two steps happen concurrently. This means it could be that T1 is first executed completely and then T2, but it could also be that they are interleaved. For example:  T1.step1 ➔ T2.step1 ➔ T1.step2 ➔ T2.step2

As you can see, this is problematic. Alice might now assume that they have less money than they actually have.

Dirty Reads are prevented with the READ_COMMITTED transaction isolation level. As there are so many scenarios where reading uncommitted data is problematic, PostgreSQL does not even allow it:

The SQL standard defines one additional level, READ UNCOMMITTED. In PostgreSQL READ UNCOMMITTED is treated as READ COMMITTED (source)

Non-repeatable Reads 🤷

When the same row is read twice in one transaction, but does not contain the same information due to a change outside of the transaction, it’s a non-repeatable read (aka read skew).

Alice likes to keep track of their financial situation. One part of that is to get the sum of their balances as well as the individual balances. However, this time she is unlucky. She reads the sum of balances before they both pay 400€ rent. After that, she reads the individual balances.

To see it yourself, you need two terminal sessions opened to your PostgreSQL server:

--  Transaction 2                                 Transaction 1
# UPDATE balances SET balance = 500;
UPDATE 2

# start transaction isolation level read committed;
START TRANSACTION
# SELECT SUM(balance)
  FROM balances
  WHERE id in ('Alice', 'Bob');
 sum
------
 1000
(1 row)

                                                   SELECT transfer_out('Alice', 400);
                                                   SELECT transfer_out('Bob', 400);
                                                   SELECT * FROM balances;
                                                     id   | balance
                                                    -------+---------
                                                    Alice |     100
                                                    Bob   |     100
# SELECT *
  FROM balances
  WHERE id in ('Alice', 'Bob');
  id   | balance
-------+---------
 Alice |     100
 Bob   |     100
(2 rows)

# END;
COMMIT

Non-repeatable Reads are prevented with the REPEATABLE_READ transaction isolation level:

# UPDATE balances SET balance = 500;
UPDATE 2

# start transaction isolation level repeatable read;
START TRANSACTION
# SELECT SUM(balance)
  FROM balances
  WHERE id in ('Alice', 'Bob');
 sum
------
 1000
(1 row)

                                                   SELECT transfer_out('Alice', 400);
                                                   SELECT transfer_out('Bob', 400);
                                                   SELECT * FROM balances;
                                                     id   | balance
                                                    -------+---------
                                                    Alice |     100
                                                    Bob   |     100
# SELECT *
  FROM balances
  WHERE id in ('Alice', 'Bob');
  id   | balance
-------+---------
 Alice |     500
 Bob   |     500
(2 rows)

# END;
COMMIT

Phantom Reads 👻

If the same query is executed twice during a transaction, but the set of rows differ, a phantom read happened. The disappeared rows are the phantoms.

Phantom Reads are prevented with the SERIALIZABLE isolation level according to the ANSI SQL-92 standard. However, the implementation of the REPEATABLE READ transaction isolation level in PostgreSQL also prevents phantom reads.

start transaction isolation level read committed;
SELECT * FROM balances;
  id   | balance
-------+---------
 Alice |     500
 Bob   |     500
(2 rows)

                                                   INSERT INTO
                                                      balances
                                                      (id, balance)
                                                   VALUES
                                                      ('Charlie', 500);

# SELECT * FROM balances;
  id     | balance
---------+---------
 Alice   |     500
 Bob     |     500
 Charlie |     500
(3 rows)

END;

Charlie is the phantom here 👻

Lost Update

When one UPDATE is lost because it is overwritten by another UPDATE of a second transaction, it’s called a lost update.

As an example, the following case. The left side and the right side are two different transactions:

start transaction isolation level read committed;
SELECT * FROM balances ORDER BY id;
  id   | balance
-------+---------
 Alice |     500
 Bob   |     500
(2 rows)

                            UPDATE balances SET balance = 100 WHERE id = 'Bob';

UPDATE balances SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 'Bob';
END;

If you are in the REPEATABLE_READ isolation level, the second UPDATE will trigger an exception:

ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update

How does Postgres implement transaction isolation levels?

Postgres uses snapshot isolation for all transaction isolation levels (source):

  • READ_COMMITTED sees a snapshot as of the start of the current statement within the transaction
  • REPEATABLE_READ sees a snapshot as of the start of the first non-transaction-control statement in the transaction.
  • SERIALIZABLE is like REPEATABLE_READ, but additionally monitors for conditions that could make the execution of a concurrent set of serializable transactions behave in a manner inconsistent with all possible serial (one at a time) executions of those transactions

Postgres uses a variant of Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) which is called Serializable Snapshot Isolation. The core idea is that every update does never overwrite data, but instead adds it to the DB with a transaction ID. When a SELECT is executed, potentially multiple versions can be selected which allows one transaction to have a consistent snapshot. The implementation of the SERIALIZABLE isolation level is complex.

Other Anomalies

If this is not enough for you, I recommend reading A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels by Berenson, Bernstein, Gray, Melton, O’Neil, and O’Neil. They go into detail and point out other anomalies. For example, a dirty write is prevented by all isolation levels (even READ_UNCOMMITTED). It’s different from a write skew. Write skews are prevented in the SERIALIZABLE isolation level in Postgres.

Summary

Here is an overview of which transaction isolation levels prevent which read phenomena:

Isolation Level Dirty Read Non-repeatable Read Phantom Read
READ_UNCOMMITTED 💩 possible 💩 possible 💩 possible
READ_COMMITTED ✅ prevented 💩 possible 💩 possible
REPEATABLE_READ ✅ prevented ✅ prevented 💩 possible
SERIALIZABLE ✅ prevented ✅ prevented ✅ prevented

Those isolation levels are defined in the SQL standard. However, various databases might give stronger guarantees. For example, the READ_UNCOMMITTED transaction isolation level is equal to the READ_COMMITTED isolation level in Postgres. Also, the REPEATABLE_READ isolation level already prevents phantom reads in Postgres.

References

I’ve read/viewed a lot in order to create this article. The most valuable resources were:

  • Vlad Mihalcea: Transactions and Concurrency Control Patterns at Devoxx on YouTube, 2017.
  • The Internals of PostgreSQL
  • Uwe Röhm: Transaction Systems in IN2267, 2014.
  • PostgreSQL Docs: Transaction Isolation
  • Berenson, Bernstein, Gray, Melton, O’Neil, and O’Neil: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, 1995. — Adrian Colyer made a nice write-up.

entry.title: Python 3.10 is Released
entry.summary:
Python 3.10 was released on the 4th of October 2021 according to PEP 619. Let’s see what’s in store for us.

Type Annotations

I absolutely love type annotations. Since Python 3.6, they are super useful. If you don’t use them already, I highly recommend you …
entry.content:
Python 3.10 was released on the 4th of October 2021 according to PEP 619. Let’s see what’s in store for us.

Type Annotations

I absolutely love type annotations. Since Python 3.6, they are super useful. If you don’t use them already, I highly recommend you to read my introduction.

Python 3.10 has improved them again! Let’s see how:

TypeGuards: Conditional Type Narrowing

PEP 647 introduces a new TypeGuard annotation. It’s backported via typing_extensions.

from typing_extensions import TypeGuard  # Before Python 3.10
from typing import TypeGuard  # With Python 3.10

Without TypeGuards, you could not find that there is an issue with this:

from typing import TypedDict, TypeGuard


class User(TypedDict):
    name: str
    email: str


def is_user(data: dict) -> TypeGuard[User]:
    return "name" in data and "email" in data


if __name__ == "__main__":
    user = {"name": "Martin", "email": "info@martin-thoma.de"}
    user = {}
    if is_user(user):
        print(user["x"])

But with the TypeGuard, you can see:

typeguard.py:17: error: TypedDict "User" has no key "x"

Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)

Neat! Now you can get rid of a couple of cast and assert calls or comments like # type: ignore.

Syntactic Sugar: Allow writing union types as X | Y ✨

Readability counts. The documentation is a lot of the reason why I love type annotations so much. PEP 604 allows you to use a more concise syntax that is easier to read:

# Before 3.10
from typing import Union


def foo() -> Union[float, str]: ...


isinstance(bar, (float, int))


# With 3.10
def foo(a: int) -> float | str: ...


isinstance(bar, float | int)

Parameter Specification Variables: Type Annotations for Decorators

Non-trivial decorators are a pain to understand once they are written. And writing type-annotations has been pretty hard. PEP 612 introduces typing.ParamSpec and typing.Concatenate.

The PEP already gives a good example for those. Imagine you wrote a decorator add_logging which executed log_to_database before the decorated function is called. The function could have any parameters — the execution of the function should not be changed. How would you annotate that?

With parameter specification variables you could do it like this:

from typing import Awaitable, Callable, ParamSpec, TypeVar

P = ParamSpec("P")
R = TypeVar("R")


def add_logging(f: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]:
    async def inner(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        await log_to_database()
        return f(*args, **kwargs)

    return inner


@add_logging
def takes_int_str(x: int, y: str) -> int:
    return x + 7


await takes_int_str(1, "A")  # Accepted
await takes_int_str("B", 2)  # Correctly rejected by the type checker

You can also add parameters or remove them with decorators. And now you can add proper types for that! Just have a look into PEP 612.

Explicit Type Aliases

PEP 613 introduces typing.TypeAlias. This helps the type checker to distinguish between module-level assignments to create constants and actual type aliases:

StrCache: TypeAlias = "Cache[str]"  # a type alias
LOG_PREFIX = "LOG[DEBUG]"  # a module constant

This helps mypy to give better error messages.

Structural Pattern Matching

Structural Pattern Matching is such a big new feature that it is covered by multiple PEPs: PEP 634 (Specification), PEP 635 (Rationale), and PEP 636 (Tutorial)!

An example from the tutorial explains it best:

match command.split():
    case ["quit"]:
        print("Goodbye!")
        quit_game()
    case ["look"]:
        current_room.describe()
    case ["get", obj]:
        character.get(obj, current_room)
    case ["go", direction]:
        current_room = current_room.neighbor(direction)
    # The rest of your commands go here

As you can see, the new keywords are match and case. The part after the match is what is evaluated. In this case, command.split() returns a list of strings. An equivalent code before structural pattern matching would be:

val: List[str] = command.split()

if val == ["quit"]:
    print("Goodbye!")
    quit_game()
elif val == ["look"]:
    current_room.describe()
elif len(val) == 2 and val[0] == "get":
    obj = val[1]
    character.get(obj, current_room)
elif len(val) == 2 and val[0] == "go":
    direction = val[1]
    current_room = current_room.neighbor(direction)

As you can see, the first example is way easier to read. There are a lot of other examples — I recommend going through this tutorial!

Better Error Messages

Python 3.10 has improved a couple of error messages. Here are just two examples, but there are many more:

I’m using the colored Python shell script to get the highlighting. In the Terminal I use ZSH and the solarized dark color theme.

Performance

Comparing performance is always hard. It depends a lot on your workload and what exactly you’re interested in. One obvious part is the startup time. The interpreter starts roughly 10% faster than Python 3.8. Also, the rendering of Django templates improved quite a bit.

Python 3.10 will be faster than 3.9 and 3.8:

Python 3.10 will be up to 10% faster: https://t.co/7ydQ4iATsN. Here's the email that I wrote to python-dev 4.5 years ago with some perf ideas: https://t.co/tuJL7yXmjZ. Thanks to @pyblogsal for picking up my patch and polishing it to get it merged. 🚀

— Yury Selivanov (@1st1) October 20, 2020

Python 3.10 is bringing a lot of cool things but how much faster is going to be? 🤔 The answer is "it depends" 😉 In the performance benchmark suite (https://t.co/RxzDk7vK33) we are seeing speedups up to 25% in some cases 🚀 How this translates to your code depends a lot. 🧵👇 pic.twitter.com/RZIfB09AlK

— Pablo Galindo Salgado (@pyblogsal) September 2, 2021

See the official speed comparison for all benchmarks.

How To Get Python 3.10

As a developer, I like to use pyenv to get the Python versions I need:

pyenv install 3.10.0
pyenv local 3.10.0

If you want to use it in production environments, you’ll be interested in Docker. The base image is 3.10, but be careful when you write this in YAML ⚠️ 3.10 might get interpreted as a float and get converted to 3.1. Write "3.10" in YAML. And maybe be more specific, e.g. 3.10-slim-bullseye.

By the way: PyPy is currently at 3.7 and AWS Lambda is at 3.9.

What Happened Before 3.10?

Many people do not use Python 3.9 yet. For this reason, you might be interested in other changes that were introduced with Python 3.9 or maybe even Python 3.8: Killer Features by Python Version Get to know what you miss when you support older Python versions: Python 2.7 to 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, 3.8 and 3.9python.plainenglish.io

Summary

Python 3.10 is great! It has …

  • Improved type annotations a lot
  • Structural Pattern Matching
  • Better error messages
  • Better performance

For a full list, see What’s New In Python 3.10.

entry.title: What developers need to know about PDF
entry.summary: Standards, functions, usage, terminology
entry.content:
PDF is a file format that was created to print in exactly the same way everywhere. It was not intended to be a format for data exchange. Nowadays, it is used in all organizations. You can create presentations with it, you can save documents like your thesis, you can create bills and forms.

Throughout my career, I had the dubious pleasure of reading PDF files multiple times. In this article, I’ll share some learnings with you. Let’s go!

PDF Format Versions

PDF is an evolving format. Adobe started developing the format in 1991, released it in 1993, and it became an ISO standard in 2008. Some important versions are:

  • PDF 1.3: JavaScript Actions, Digital signatures
  • PDF 1.4: Transparency, JBIG2Decode was introduced
  • PDF 1.5: JPXDecode, XFA was introduced, HTML 4 Form format
  • PDF 1.6: OpenType font support, interactive 3D documents
  • PDF 1.7: Basis for parts of PDF/A-2
  • PDF 2.0: XFA was deprecated

Image-Only vs Searchable vs Digitally-created

When you use a scanner, you get an image. The format of the image file could be JPG or PDF. However, the PDF simply contains the image. You cannot copy the text and you cannot search within the document. Search engines will have a harder time finding the contents. Such PDFs are called image-only PDFs.

You can apply optical character recognition (OCR) to an image. Machine Learning algorithms try to recognize the characters and put them behind the image. The resulting PDF still looks the same as the image-only PDF, but now you can search for content. The OCR algorithm might have made a mistake, so you might not be able to copy everything and some things you copy might be wrong. Such PDFs are called searchable PDFs. Many scanners can directly create searchable PDFs.

You can create a PDF via Microsoft Word or other document writing tools. When you do this, then the resulting PDF will have text which others can copy. It is easy to search content within the PDF with standard PDF viewers. The reason for that is that the data is directly within the PDF. The digitally-created PDF is sometimes also called digitally-born or a True PDF.

Archivability: PDF/A

PDF is perceived as static content, similar to a piece of paper. However, there are two reasons why one PDF might look different on different devices or at different times:

  1. Active Content: PDF can contain JavaScript and PostScript
  2. Attachments: The attachments could contain anything

To fix this issue, the standards PDF/A-1, PDF/A-2, and PDF/A-3 were developed. All of them are PDF files, but they are restricted to be suitable for long-term archives.

PDF/A-1 is based on PDF 1.4 and parts of PDF/A-2 are based on PDF 1.7.

There is software that can automatically convert files to PDF/A, but it is not possible to guarantee for all cases that the resulting file looks exactly the same as the original. It’s a good idea to check if the software vendor you are using is a member of the PDF Association.

Universal Accessibility: PDF/UA

People with disabilities also want to read PDF files. To help assistive tools like screen readers, semantics need to be added. The PDF/UA (universal accessibility) standard is similar to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. For example, images need to have alternative text which describes their content. PDF tags should group the content of the PDF file into semantic sections.

If you want to know more, I recommend reading A Technical Introduction to PDF/UA.

Printing: PDF/X

PDF/X is a standard based on PDF, restricting it to make it more useful for printing.

  • PDF/X-1a was based on PDF 1.3
  • PDF/X-3: Color management
  • PDF/X-4: Transparency
  • PDF/X-5: More flexibility
  • PDF/X-6: Based on PDF 2.0

A good explanation is given in PDF/X in a Nutshell.

Variable Data and Transactional Printing: PDF/VT

PDF/VT is based on PDF/X and is good for invoices and advertisement. Imagine a PDF with complex graphics, but one part is just your name in it. Instead of re-creating the PDF all the time with only this string changing, the PDF just contains a variable for it.

The best explanation I have seen is by prepressure.com and by Dov Isaacs in his talk “A Technical Introduction to PDF/VT”.

Engineering: PDF/E

PDF/E is for Engineering and pretty specialized as you can see with this quote from Wikipedia:

[PDF/E is] for the creation of documents used in geospatial, construction and manufacturing workflows and is based on the PDF Reference version 1.6 […].

PDF and Python

I spent a lot of time diving into the various libraries to interact with PDF files in Python. The following should give you a brief overview of the libraries I have worked with.

Reading PDF files with Python

Do you want to know how to extract text from a PDF file? I got you:

PyMuPDF is based on the C-library MuPDF which is dual-licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License and commercial permissive license.

You can read the text of a PDF like this:

import fitz  # this is pymupdf

with fitz.open("my.pdf") as doc:
    text = ""
    for page in doc:
        text += page.get_text()

print(text)

Acceptable alternatives might be:

  • pdfminer.six: It’s a pure Python module
  • PyPDF3 (GitHub): Although the last uploaded version is from 2021, I’m uncertain if this is more maintenance or actually actively developed🤔 I also don’t know anybody who uses this, and the number of GitHub stars are suspiciously low.

The following are projects I recommend NOT to use for text extraction:

  • PyPDF2: A lot of tutorials still use this, but the project was dead: the last update was from 2016. Update: In April 2022, I became the maintainer of PyPDF2 and in December 2022 we moved it back to pypdf. Use pypdf (see The Python PDF Ecosystem in 2024).
  • PyPDF4: This project never really started. There was just one release and it was in 2018.
  • pdfminer: The last updated version is from 2019. The project is dead.
  • pikepdf is based on the C++ library qpdf which is Apache 2.0 licensed. The project makes a pretty good impression, but pikepdf doesn’t support reading text from PDF files.

Reading Tables from PDF files

I’ve spent quite some time with this problem and it’s ridiculously hard. You have to know that tables are not a single semantic object in PDF. They are rather absolutely positioned text. In the worst case, every single letter could be absolutely positioned. That’s just a nightmare, especially if you have non-trivial structures like tables within tables, merged cells, invisible borders, text overflowing a column, …

Having said that, there is Camelot and the Java project Tabula with the Python wrapper tabula-py. I’ve found examples for both where it worked well, examples where either of them or both failed. It’s simply a hard problem 🤷

Creating PDF files with Python

There are a couple of different ways and I cannot say that I’m really happy with any of them.

When it comes to the quality of the produced PDF, I was most happy with going over LaTeX to PDF. The results LaTeX can generate are simply beautiful; have a look at my LaTeX examples. However, calling pdflatex via a subprocess just feels wrong. It is a pain to set LaTeX up when you want the full TeX Live support. It worked well, though.

A simpler approach converts HTML to PDF. I was reasonably happy with wkhtmltopdf. I’ve also seen pdfkit to make using wkhtmltopdf easier. I’ve also stumbled a couple of years ago over weasyprint, but that didn’t work for me. I don’t remember why.

Reportlab is a common approach to generate PDF files directly from Python. As an alternative, I would give pikepdf a shot if I needed to do this again.

entry.title: Performance Testing for Web Services
entry.summary: What it is, aspects to consider, and tools you can use
entry.content:
We all want software to be reliable and use minimum resources. Those are non-functional requirements and they need to be tested. In this article, we focus on web services. This means requirements like minimum energy consumption or mobile network usage are irrelevant.

After reading the article you will have a basic understanding of topics that touch performance testing and know some tools that you can use for testing web services.

In which performance aspects are we interested?

We might be interested in three different aspects of performance. Depending on what you’re interested in, you will look at different metrics.

  • Speed: How fast does the page load? For speed you might look at page rendering times, at response times of APIs, or throughput for bigger file transfers.
  • Stability: Does the system behave normally? For stability you will look at error rates.
  • Scalability: Which resources do we need to increase and by which amount if the number of our users doubles? For scalability you will look at resource utilization in comparison to different loads.

Which Resources might be Bottlenecks?

If you want to find bottlenecks for web services, I would look at:

  • Database load: Is the amount of requests we send to the database reasonable? Are the requests themselves fast to execute?
  • Peak memory usage: Is there anything heavy you need to compute? How does that scale?
  • Hardware: I’ve heard of cases where the network card was a limiting factor (example), although this might be less of an issue with cloud hosted machines.
  • CPU: When CPU utilization is too high, everything will break apart.
  • Disk space: Log files or files which are generated could kill the service on longer runs.
  • Connections: There might be a maximum number of HTTP connections / DB connections. For Postgres, the max_connections is 100. nginx workers are limited to 512 concurrent connections by default (source).

Performance Testing Types

Now that we know what potential issues are, we should talk about common performance testing types. The most common ones are load testing, stress testing, and soak testing.

Load Testing

The purpose of load testing is to see the behavior of the tested system under an expected load. You don’t want to break the system here, but you want to have a load which you might get during “rush hours”. Is the application able to perform as expected under the anticipated load?

Think of a hospital or an airport where you make emergency tests, but with people who know that it will be a test. You still want to get a high, but not completely unreasonably high number of people in the test.

Stress Testing

After load testing we know how the system behaves under anticipated load. Let’s break stuff. When we test the application under extreme load to see when/where/how things break, we call it stress testing.

Is the system stable under load? Do users see failures? Where is the upper limit of the system? Where are limits of the system? Does the system recover after failure? When it fails, is only the system’s availability affected or also its correctness?

Soak Testing

Soak testing is trying to answer the question how the system performs over a longer time. We want to confirm that the system is reliable over a long period of time.

Things that could go wrong and be discovered under soak testing:

  • DB Connection exhaustion
  • Unexpected restarts
  • Resource leaks, e.g. memory leaks
  • Logs or other files that bloat the system

Load Profiles

Think of a web service in the context of performance testing as a street system. People want to get from A to B. They need to go through several streets. Some have 5 lanes, others just one. Some allow them to go at 130 km/h (80 mph), others just at 50 km/h (30mph). Depending on the timing, there might be a congestion. If there is a bottleneck where you can drive fast, it might be highly unlikely that you need to wait for somebody to go through it. But the more people are in the road system, the higher the chances are that some people need to wait.

The road system is your web service. The bottleneck might be a blocking resource call such as a database transaction under a high transaction isolation level. The speed is how fast the transaction is executing.

Testing Tools

There are tons of performance testing and profiling tools. I’ll just briefly mention a couple that I’ve either used in the past (Apache ab, Locust) or want to use (Apache JMeter, K6).

Apache JMeter

Apache JMeter is a protocol-based load testing tool. JMeter simulates traffic and concurrent users. It looks similar to Locust, but more feature-rich.

Apache ab

Apache ab is an HTTP server benchmarking tool. As such, it covers way less of your system than Apache JMeter — just the HTTP server. I’m pretty certain that the HTTP server isn’t the problem most of the time.

Stress and resource limits

If you want to see how the system behaves when it hits resource limits, you can artificially reduce the resources your application has or apply stress to the system.

Locust

Locust is a performance testing tool which lets you define web users that send HTTP requests. Locust automatically measures the response times and denotes failures / successes. You do this via a locustfile.py which you simply execute with Python. It looks like this:

from locust import HttpUser, task, between


class QuickstartUser(HttpUser):
    wait_time = between(1, 2)

    def on_start(self):
        self.client.post(
            "/login",
            json={"username": "foo", "password": "bar"},
        )

    @task
    def hello_world(self):
        self.client.get("/hello")
        self.client.get("/world")

    @task(3)
    def view_item(self):
        for item_id in range(10):
            self.client.get(f"/item?id={item_id}", name="/item")

Executing locust in the folder with the locustfile.py starts a local web server so that you can interact with Locust via the browser.

When you start Locust, you can specify how many users you would like to spawn and how fast the users should be generated (“hatched”):

The first thing you will notice is the statistics. For every endpoint, you see the number of requests that were made against that endpoint. Locust measures how many of those requests failed, the response time, and the response size. From the response times, it shows you the minimum, median, average, 90-percentile and the maximum.

In this example, you can see that the /users/registration endpoint failed a couple of times. It also has a pretty high response time — both, for the maximum and the 90%ile. As the minimum response time is pretty low, this could be an indicator that this endpoint runs into a bottleneck.

Next, we should look at the failures:

Locust lets you define specific messages via response.failure('failure message') and shows them to you here. It also captures more general issues.

Looking at the charts can help you to identify breaking points:

It takes a few seconds as the number of users and the number of requests increase until the response times increase as well.

K6

K6 is a load testing tool. You can write performance tests as JavaScript files. You can record usage with a Chrome plugin and visualize the results in Grafana. It seems super flexible and I’m looking forward to using it 😀

Digging into Performance Issues

When we identified performance issues in a test run, we also want to do something about it. We want to pin-point where the issue comes from so that we can fix it. Here are some tools and techniques I found useful in the past.

Counting Queries

ORMs are amazing, but it can happen way too easily to run into the (n+1)-issue. It’s quite easy to detect if you write unit tests for those parts and also test for the number of executed SQL queries.

Linear Microservice Cascade

If you use a service which in turn uses another service which uses another service …. well, then you get the load time of the sum of all. This is an architectural issue. It might require heavy rewrites or a lot of caching.

Measure Memory Usage

When working on machine learning / data science topics, it sometimes happened that I needed to multiply large matrices in a production system. To ease my mind, I measured the peak memory usage with valgrind and visualized it with kcachegrind. In the Python world, memory_profiler helped me. Those tools are called “memory profilers” and they can show all kinds of things, including call-graphs like this:

Setting resource limits artificially low also helped me once to identify where memory becomes an issue.

Front-End Performance

I’ve seen people using Google Lighthouse to find performance issues in the front-end:

Using Lighthouse To Improve Page Load Performance | Web Lighthouse is an automated tool for improving the quality of your site. You give it a URL, and it provides a list of…

It’s typically run from the Chrome dev tools, but you can integrate Lighthouse in your CI and run it automatically as well!

Database Speedups

You might run into the situation that you need to speed up your database. Don’t worry, here are 8 hints what you could try:

8 Techniques To Speed up Your Database “If everything seems under control, you’re not going fast enough”

How many users do we support?

This is a question every web service needs to answer. Before you can give a number, you need to know the following:

  • Realistic Scenario: Are the virtual users behaving similar enough to the real users?
  • Timeouts: When is a request counted as a failure? Are 3 seconds response times still ok? Are 300 seconds response time ok? Where is the threshold?
  • Maximum failure rate: How many failures are you willing to accept? Having it as a rate, e.g. “failures in the last 5 minutes”, enables you to run soak tests.

Summary

You’ve learned the difference between load testing, stress testing, and soak testing. You know that not only speed, but also failures and recovery are important. You know that you can use Apache JMeter, Locust, or K6 to get started. Let’s start experimenting!

entry.title: Bugs, Issues, Flaws, Faults, Failures, Errors, and Defects
entry.summary: So many things that can go wrong
entry.content:
Bug, issue, flaw, fault, failure, error, and defect are often used synonymously, but there are differences:

  • An error is a mistake, e.g. a programming error or a usage error. Not every mistake leads to follow-up issues.
  • A defect is an error found during the development phase whereas a bug is a defect found during testing phase. Not all programming errors are detectable. Hence not all errors cause defects/bugs.
  • A failure is when the system does not meet its requirements. It’s an error that reached a user.
  • A fault is the cause of a failure. It could be a programming error or it could be misuse of the system by the user.
  • An issue can be anything — even something that was specified and is correct according to the specification. It might be something that bothers the user or something that makes development harder. It could be a design choice that leads to errors.
  • A flaw typically refers to an issue in the architecture of the software or the design / specification of the overall system. Flaws are not directly wrong, but cause issues.

For example, if you put Diesel in a gasoline car, the car will stop working. The fact that the motor isn’t working anymore is a failure. The fault was to put Diesel in the car. Users and testers typically report failures, developers need to find the faults.

Sources: 360logica.com, ISTQB foundation level material, Understanding what Fault, Error and Failure mean, Difference between bug, defect and flaw, Security bugs and flaws

Let’s use all of those words in one scenario: Imagine a car driver who goes to a mechanic complaining that the car does not run. The user reports a failure. The car failed to run. The technician inspects the car and confirms it. He figures out that there is Diesel in the gasoline engine — he identified the cause: It’s the user’s fault — the cause of the failure is that they put Diesel in the gasoline engine! Now we try to find the reason why the fault was made. It was human error — the driver was not paying attention. But it’s an issue that you can put Diesel in a gasoline engine at all.

Let’s look at some examples of interesting or common programming errors!

Unit Errors — Imperial vs Metric

When you deal with physical systems, units matter. It matters if you drive 100 miles or 100 km per hour. The Mars Climate Orbiter team learned that the hard way: One team used imperial units while the other one used metric units. This mismatch in communication between two software components brought the spacecraft too close to Mars, where it was destroyed in the atmosphere. It’s a loss of 327.6 million USD.

This type of error can be prevented by using unit libraries like Python’s pint that do unit conversions for you. Once again, strong types are the rescue 😉

Off-by-One Errors

Off-by-one errors are super common: Less than or less than or equal? Greater than or greater than or equal? Less or greater? They are logic errors that can often be found by calling the function with example input and checking the actual output against the expected output. Those off-by-one errors can also easily lead to infinite loops.

Off-by-one errors can be detected by good unit tests. Mutation testing can help to make the test suite detect those:

Mutation Testing with Python Test the tests — automatically, by applying common mistakes

Race Conditions

A race condition occurs when two or more threads / processes work on the same data. Suddenly the timing when which part of which process executes becomes important. If you’re lucky, it could be that everything works as desired. But if the timing is bad, several phenomena can occur:

  • Dirty Read
  • Non-repeatable reads
  • Phantom Read

In the database world you can choose between different transaction isolation levels to prevent those, such as REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE (more details).

Those errors are notoriously hard to find, because they depend on the timing of multiple systems. For this reason, they are also sometimes called Heisenbugs: If you inspect them, they are gone.

Uninitialized resources

Uninitialized resources (e.g. Nullpointer Exception or KeyError in Python) I think are mostly covered by line coverage in unit tests and type checking tools like mypy.

Non-functional issues

One of the most common non-functional bugs is that the code is too slow. You can get a grasp of this with pytest-benchmark, but the problem is that it depends on the hardware and what you run at the same time on the machine.

Another one I see often with browsers is that it is too memory-intensive. I guess that is a problem for smartphones as well.

Speaking of smartphones, too power-intensive is certainly another one.

Human Error

Stating the root cause of a failure is human error is lazy in my opinion. It often means we give up on improving the system. However, I think distinguishing four types of “human error” might lead to more interesting conclusions:

  • Slips — Failures of Attention: Maybe we need to make a warning more prominent, remove clutter from an interface, or have more people for the job.
  • Lapses — Failures of Memory: If people forgot to do something, it might be that they have too many things to remember or that it was too long ago. Having training more often or simplifying the work could help.
  • Mistakes — Unintentional decision making errors: If people break a rule or procedure, they might lack knowledge or understanding about the process.
  • Violation — Intentionally doing the wrong thing: If people break a rule or procedure on purpose, they might not be aware of the consequences or their normal workflow would be significantly slower if they followed the rules all the time.

The UK Health and Safety Executive created an overview for Understanding Human Failure.

entry.title: API Testing with Insomnia
entry.summary: Boost your productivity and make tests easier to reproduce
entry.content:
Testing is a crucial part of software development. It comes in different flavors such as unit testing, stress testing, acceptance testing, smoke testing. “Just giving it a shot” is probably the simplest of them all, but crucial to be convinced that things work as they should.

After reading this article, you will know how to use Insomnia for API testing. We will go through the request collection interface of Insomnia, look at environments, and request chaining. Let’s get started!

The Basics

If you don’t know what an endpoint, HTTP methods, or status codes are, please feel free to refresh your knowledge:

API Testing with HTTPie Testing is a crucial part of software development. It comes in different flavors such as unit testing, stress testing…

Getting started with Insomnia

You can download and install Insomnia for free (link). There is a paid version with additional features, but you will not need it for now.

First, create a “request collection”:

Create a GET request

Click on “New Request” or hit Ctrl + N and enter “Get names gender” as the request name. Enter https://api.genderize.io/ for the URL and go to the “Query” tab. Enter “name” as “New name” and “Andreas” as value. Hit the purple “Send” button:

The Headers Tab

Click on the “Headers” tab to see the response headers:

The Timeline Tab
